docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 5 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Yoga Taraṅgiṇī: Yoga Traditions. A taraṅgiṇī is a river, “she who has waves”, and the image suits the subject. Yoga has never been a single system. It has meant Patañjali’s meditative discipline, the Gītā’s yogas of action, devotion and knowledge, the subtle-body practices of the Tantras, the forceful techniques of Haṭha Yoga and, in the last century, a posture practice that has spread across the world.

The chapters follow these currents roughly in the order in which they arose: the Upaniṣadic, epic and Purāṇic background (Chapter 1); Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra, its eight limbs and its commentators (Chapter 2); the Gītā’s yogas of action and devotion (Chapter 3) and the Advaita tradition’s uneasy relation to yoga (Chapter 4); the yoga of the Tantras and the subtle body they devised (Chapters 5–6); Haṭha Yoga, which inherited that body, with its texts, its ascetic orders and its reception among Sufis, Mughals, Sikhs and poets in Tamil and Marathi (Chapter 7); breath, meditation and sound (Chapters 8–10); and modern yoga (Chapter 11).

We have tried to combine respect for the tradition with historical honesty. Dates follow the academic chronology, with traditional dates labelled as such. Sanskrit passages are given only where their wording and source could be confirmed. We distinguish what the texts claim, what later tradition added, and what modern research has shown. Practices with health implications carry safety notes; nothing here is medical advice. Caste and the abuse of power by modern gurus are addressed directly.

This is a work of synthesis for the general reader and student. Every quotation should be checked against a critical edition before it is relied on, and specialists will find much to refine.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Texts and Editions
docs.text: References to primary texts give the conventional chapter and verse (or sūtra) numbers, and the numbering systems followed are these. The Yoga Sūtra is cited in the common numbering of Woods’s translation (Woods 1914); the first chapter has been critically edited by Maas (Maas 2006), and the work’s history is surveyed in Maas (2013) and Larson and Bhattacharya (2008). The Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā is cited in the vulgate of 389 verses, as in the Kaivalyadhama edition (Svātmārāma 1970); the GRETIL e-text numbers most of chapter 1 two higher, and some readings quoted here follow e-texts and should be checked against that edition. The Gheraṇḍa and Śiva Saṃhitās follow Mallinson’s editions and translations (Mallinson 2004, 2007); the Amṛtasiddhi, the Dattātreyayogaśāstra, the Khecarīvidyā and the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati follow the critical editions cited in Chapter 7. The Bhagavad Gītā is cited in the vulgate numbering used by Śaṅkara (Śaṅkarācārya 1997), the Upaniṣads in their standard numbering (the Kaṭha by chapter, section and verse, with the continuous numbering in brackets), and the Ṛgveda by book, hymn and verse. Translations are free renderings that follow the cited editions and translations; they are not substitutes for them.

docs.title: Transliteration and Dates
docs.text: Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). Words from Hindi, Marathi and Tamil are transliterated in the forms customary in scholarship (Tamil, for example, Tirumūlar, Cittar, vāci); Arabic and Persian titles are given in a simplified scholarly form. Familiar modern names of people, places and institutions keep their usual English spelling (Krishnamacharya, Rishikesh, Kaivalyadhama). Dates follow the mainstream academic chronology of the series; where a traditional date differs, it is given second and labelled as traditional. The principal dates are collected in the Chronology at the end of the volume.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: What is Yoga?
docs.text:
Yoga Sūtra 1.1

atha yogānuśāsanam Now begins the authoritative instruction on Yoga. — Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 1.1

docs.title: 1.1 The Eternal Quest
docs.text:
For well over two thousand years, thinkers and practitioners in South Asia have asked how the restless mind can be stilled, how suffering can be ended, and how freedom (mokṣa, kaivalya, nirvāṇa) can be attained. Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain ascetics all developed disciplines of meditation, breath and bodily restraint in answer to these questions. The family of such disciplines that came to be called Yoga is the subject of this volume.

Yoga is not merely a system of physical exercises, as it is often portrayed in the contemporary world. In its classical sources it is a soteriological discipline — a method for liberation — that works on the body (śarīra), the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind (manas, citta) and the intellect (buddhi), with the aim of realising the true nature of the self (puruṣa or ātman, according to the school). Yoga has never been a single system: the word covers Patañjali’s meditative darśana, the Gītā’s disciplines of action, knowledge and devotion, Tantric ritual-meditative practice, medieval Haṭha Yoga and the posture-based practice of the modern world. One aim of this volume is to keep these strands distinct while showing how they borrowed from one another.

Key Point: The Many Dimensions of Yoga

Across its history the word yoga has named:

  • Darśana (Philosophy) — one of the six classical Brahmanical schools, closely allied to Sāṃkhya

  • Sādhana (Practice) — a structured discipline of self-transformation

  • Mārga (Path) — in the Gītā and later Hinduism, any disciplined way to liberation (karma, bhakti, jñāna)

  • Modern practice — since the twentieth century, a global posture-and-breath practice often pursued for health

docs.title: 1.2 Etymology of Yoga
docs.text:
The word Yoga is derived from the Sanskrit root yuj, whose basic meaning is “to yoke,” “to harness,” or “to join.” The Dhātupāṭha (the list of verbal roots associated with Pāṇini’s grammar) records more than one root yuj, and the commentators exploited this. Vyāsa’s Yogabhāṣya on Yoga Sūtra 1.1 glosses the word simply as yogaḥ samādhiḥ, “yoga is concentration,” taking it from yuj in the sense of samādhi rather than “union”.

Definition: Etymological Dimensions of Yoga

The root yuj yields three principal meanings:

  1. Yuj samādhau — To concentrate, to absorb, to enter into samādhi

  2. Yujir yoge — To yoke, to unite, to join

  3. Yuj saṃyamane — To control, to discipline, to restrain

Classical Yoga (Patañjali and Vyāsa) favours the first sense; theistic and Vedāntic texts favour “union” (of the individual self with the supreme); the Gītā often uses yoga in the broader sense of “discipline” or “method”.

The word yoga is cognate with the English “yoke” (from the Proto-Indo-European root *yeug-), the Greek zugon, and the Latin iugum. In early Vedic usage it refers to yoking draught animals to a chariot; the meditative sense develops later, in the Upaniṣads and the epic.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Definitions Across the Tradition
docs.text:
Different schools and texts have defined Yoga according to their own emphasis and perspective. The following are among the most celebrated definitions:

Patañjali’s Definition — Yoga Sūtra 1.2

yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ Yoga is the cessation (nirodha) of the fluctuations (vṛtti) of the mind-stuff (citta).

This is perhaps the most widely cited definition, establishing Yoga as fundamentally a discipline of the mind. The term citta here refers to the entire field of consciousness, including manas (the thinking mind), buddhi (the discriminative intellect), and ahaṃkāra (the ego-sense) (Table 1.1).

The Bhagavad Gītā defines yoga quite differently, in terms of action rather than stillness: “equanimity is called yoga” (samatvaṃ yoga ucyate, 2.48) and “yoga is skill in action” (yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam, 2.50). Both verses are discussed with the Gītā’s Karma Yoga in Chapter 3.

Kaṭha Upaniṣad Definition

tāṃ yogam iti manyante sthirām indriya-dhāraṇām They consider Yoga to be the firm holding (restraint) of the senses. — Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.11 (= 6.11)

Table 1.1. Definitions of Yoga Across Key Texts Source Definition Emphasis Yoga Sūtra 1.2 Cessation of mental fluctuations Mind control Gītā 2.48 Equanimity in action Equipoise Gītā 2.50 Skill in action Perfection in karma Kaṭha Upaniṣad Firm restraint of senses Sense mastery Viṣṇu Purāṇa Contact of the Self with the Supreme Divine union Yogayājñavalkya Union of the individual self (jīvātman) with the supreme self Spiritual union Haṭha texts Haṭha = “force”; a later esoteric etymology reads ha (sun) + ṭha (moon) Effortful method

docs.title: 1.3 Historical Overview of Yoga
docs.text: The history of Yoga is long and its early stages are poorly documented. Dates in this volume follow the mainstream academic chronology, with traditional dates labelled as such, and are collected in the Chronology at the end of the book. The older syntheses, Mircea Eliade’s Yoga: Immortality and Freedom and Georg Feuerstein’s The Yoga Tradition, remain stimulating, but their chronology, especially for Haṭha Yoga, has been overtaken by the editions of the last two decades (Eliade 1958; Feuerstein 1998); Stuart Sarbacker’s survey reflects the current state of research (Sarbacker 2021). The following broad phases may be identified (White 2014; Samuel 2008).

docs.title: 1.3.1 Indus and Vedic Background (before c. 500 BCE)
docs.text:
The so-called Paśupati seal from Mohenjo-daro (Harappan civilisation, c. 2600–1900 BCE) shows a horned figure seated with heels drawn together, and since Sir John Marshall’s excavation reports it has often been called a “proto-Yogi” or “proto-Śiva”. The identification is speculative: the Indus script is undeciphered, the posture may be a conventional way of depicting a seated figure, and many specialists doubt that the image tells us anything about meditative practice (Samuel 2008). It should be read as a possible, not an established, early trace (Figure 1.1).

Figure 1.1. A modern replica of the so-called Paśupati seal from Mohenjo-daro (the original is a small steatite seal, c. 2600–1900 BCE). Its interpretation as a figure in yogic posture is disputed. Photo: Aadrit28, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

In the Ṛg Veda (composed c. 1500–1200 BCE) there is no systematic Yoga, but there are references to ascetic heat (tapas), to inspired seers, and to ecstatic figures who stand outside ordinary society, such as the long-haired keśin of ṚV 10.136 (see Section 1.4).

docs.title: 1.3.2 The Upaniṣadic Period (c. 700–200 BCE)
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads represent a decisive turning point in the evolution of Yoga. In the later verse Upaniṣads (the Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara, probably of the last few centuries BCE), Yoga is for the first time explicitly named and described as a discipline for attaining spiritual knowledge (jñāna) and liberation (mokṣa).

The Kaṭha Upaniṣad presents the famous chariot metaphor: the body is the chariot, the Ātman is the rider, the intellect (buddhi) is the charioteer, the mind (manas) is the reins, and the senses (indriyāṇi) are the horses. Yoga is the means by which the charioteer controls the horses and brings the chariot safely to its destination.

The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad provides one of the earliest detailed descriptions of meditation technique, including posture, breath control, and the withdrawal of the senses. The Maitrī Upaniṣad, whose date is debated, describes a six-limbed Yoga (ṣaḍaṅga yoga) that parallels Patañjali’s eight-limbed system.

docs.title: 1.3.3 The Epic and Classical Period (c. 400 BCE – 500 CE)
docs.text: This period witnessed the flowering of Yoga into distinct and well-articulated paths. It was also the period in which Buddhist and Jain contemplative disciplines were being systematised (Section 9.10; Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā); the vocabulary of meditation was shared across these traditions, and Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra in particular shows clear engagement with Buddhist ideas (Bronkhorst 1993).

docs.title: The Bhagavad Gītā
docs.text: The Bhagavad Gītā, set within the Mahābhārata, did more than any other text to present yoga as a discipline for people living in the world. Kṛṣṇa’s teaching uses yoga in several senses. The Gītā itself names two disciplines, the jñānayoga of the Sāṃkhyas and the karmayoga of the yogins (BG 3.3); later readers found in it three, of action (above all BG chs 3 and 5), devotion (BG chs 9 and 12) and knowledge (BG chs 2 and 13), and from Vivekānanda onwards these became three of the “four yogas” of modern Hindu teaching (Section 1.9). The Gītā presents them as complementary rather than exclusive, suited to people of different natures (svabhāva); they are treated in Chapters 3 and 4.

docs.title: Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras
docs.text: The most systematic yoga text of the classical period is the Yoga Sūtras of Patañjali. Philipp Maas has argued that the sūtras and the earliest commentary (the Bhāṣya) form a single work, the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, composed c. 325–425 CE; older scholarship placed the sūtras anywhere between the 2nd century BCE and the 3rd century CE (Maas 2013). The work systematised diverse yogic teachings into 195 or 196 concise aphorisms (sūtras; the count varies slightly between editions) arranged in four chapters (pādas). Since Vivekānanda it has been treated as the foundational text of “Rāja Yoga”; it is discussed in detail in Chapter 2.

docs.title: 1.3.4 The Tantric Period (c. 500–1200 CE)
docs.text: The Tantric movement, whose earliest surviving scriptures date from around the 5th–6th centuries CE (Sanderson 2009), developed new forms of Yoga that treated the body as a map of the cosmos and a site of divine power. The Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava and Buddhist Tantric traditions developed elaborate systems of practice involving mantra, ya­ntra, nyāsa, visualisation of the subtle body, and (in some Śākta lineages) kuṇḍalinī.

docs.title: 1.3.5 The Haṭha Yoga Period (c. 11th–18th centuries CE)
docs.text: Haṭha Yoga — a discipline of physical techniques (mudrā, bandha, prāṇāyāma, later many āsanas) aimed at controlling breath and the vital fluid (bindu) — first appears in texts of the 11th–13th centuries such as the Amṛtasiddhi, which comes from a Buddhist Tantric milieu, and the Vaiṣṇava Dattātreyayogaśāstra (Mallinson and Singleton 2017; Mallinson 2011). It was later associated above all with the Nātha ascetics, who claim Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha as founders. The Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā of Svātmārāma (c. 1450 CE) compiled these earlier works; it was followed by the Śiva Saṃhitā (c. 15th century), the Haṭharatnāvalī (17th century) and the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā (c. 1700). These texts are discussed in Chapter 7.

docs.title: 1.3.6 The Modern Period (19th Century Onwards)
docs.text: The modern revival of Yoga began in the late 19th century. Swāmī Vivekānanda spoke at the Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago in 1893 and published Rāja Yoga (1896), which presented Patañjali’s Yoga to Western readers. In the 20th century teachers such as T. Krishnamacharya, Swāmī Śivānanda, Swāmī Kuvalayānanda, B.K.S. Iyengar and Pattabhi Jois made Yoga a global practice (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 1.4 Yoga in the Vedic Literature: A Deeper Exploration
docs.text: The Vedic background of Yoga is real but indirect. The Saṃhitās do not describe a yogic method, but they contain ideas — ascetic heat, inspired vision, the vital breaths — that later Yoga took up and reinterpreted.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Yoga in the Ṛg Veda
docs.text:
The Ṛg Veda, the oldest Vedic collection (composed c. 1500–1200 BCE according to the academic consensus; some Indian traditional authors propose much earlier dates), contains hymns that later tradition read as allusions to meditative and yogic practice. The concept of tapas (austerity, inner heat) is central to the Vedic worldview. In Ṛg Veda 10.129, the celebrated Nāsadīya Sūkta (Hymn of Creation), the creative impulse of the universe is attributed to tapas:

Ṛg Veda 10.129.3

tama āsīt tamasā gūḷham agre 'prake­taṃ salilaṃ sarvam ā idam tucchyenābhv apihitaṃ yad āsīt tapasas tan mahinājāyataikam Darkness was hidden by darkness in the beginning; all this was an undistinguished sea. That One which was concealed by the void — by the power of tapas (creative heat) was that One born.

The hymn to the Keśin (the long-haired ascetic, ṚV 10.136) provides one of the earliest glimpses of a yogic practitioner. The Keśin is described as one who has drunk the cup of Viṣa (interpreted by some as the poison of worldly experience, by others as a sacred intoxicant), who rides the wind, and who perceives things invisible to ordinary mortals. This figure bears striking resemblance to later descriptions of the accomplished yogi.

Ṛg Veda 10.136.2–3

munayo vāta-raśanāḥ piśaṅgā vasate malā vātasyānu dhrājiṃ yanti yad devāso avikṣata unmaditā mauneyena vātāṃ ā tasthimā vayam śarīred asmākaṃ yūyaṃ martāso abhi paśyatha The sages (muni), girdled with wind, wear soiled garments of tawny hue. They follow the rushing of the wind when the gods have entered them. “Exhilarated by our silence (mauneya), we have mounted the winds. You mortals see only our bodies.”

docs.title: 1.4.2 Yoga in the Upaniṣads of the Vedic Schools
docs.text:
The first descriptions of a yogic method come not from the Saṃhitās but from Upaniṣads transmitted by particular Vedic schools. The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, which belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, contains perhaps the earliest systematic description of yogic practice, with instructions on posture, breath control and meditation:

Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8

trir unnataṃ sthāpya samaṃ śarīraṃ hṛdīndriyāṇi manasā saṃniveśya brahmoḍupena pratareta vidvān srotāṃsi sarvāṇi bhayāvahāni Holding the body steady with the three (chest, neck, and head) erect, causing the senses and the mind to enter the heart, the wise one should cross over all the fear-bringing currents by means of the raft of Brahman.

The next verse (2.9) tells the practitioner to restrain the breaths and to hold the mind attentively, “as one holds a chariot yoked to unruly horses”: it is among the earliest descriptions of breath-control as a technique of meditation (Chapter 8). The Atharvaveda Saṃhitā, for its part, contains hymns on healing and on the vital breath, among them a hymn in praise of Prāṇa (Śaunaka recension 11.4), but no method of practice. The Praśna Upaniṣad, transmitted in the Atharvaveda tradition, discusses the five prāṇas and their functions, a teaching that became foundational for later prāṇāyāma theory. Table 1.2 keeps the two layers apart: the hymns of the Saṃhitās supply ideas, the Upaniṣads the first methods.

Table 1.2. Yoga-Related Ideas in the Vedic Saṃhitās and in the Upaniṣads of the Vedic Schools Text Vedic school Yoga-related content Saṃhitās: ideas, but no method Keśin Sūkta (ṚV 10.136) Ṛgveda Ecstatic asceticism; wind-riding; trance Nāsadīya Sūkta (ṚV 10.129) Ṛgveda Tapas as creative principle Hiraṇyagarbha Sūkta (ṚV 10.121) Ṛgveda The “golden embryo”; later tradition (Mahābhārata, Vācaspati Miśra) names Hiraṇyagarbha as the first teacher of Yoga Hymn to Prāṇa (AVŚ 11.4) Atharvaveda Praise of the vital breath Upaniṣads: the first methods Śvetāśvatara Up. Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Systematic meditation; posture; breath control Kaṭha Up. Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Chariot metaphor; Yoga defined; sense control Maitrī Up. Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Six-limbed yoga Praśna Up. Atharvaveda Pañca Prāṇa; physiology of the vital breath Māṇḍūkya Up. Atharvaveda Four states of consciousness; analysis of Oṃ Chāndogya Up. Sāmaveda Tat tvam asi; meditation on the Ud­gītha

docs.title: 1.4.3 The Yoga Upaniṣads
docs.text:
Beyond the principal Upaniṣads, there exists a collection of about twenty Yoga Upaniṣads — minor Upaniṣads specifically devoted to yogic practices and philosophy. Despite the Upaniṣadic name, these are medieval works: several borrow from Haṭha texts such as the Yogabīja and Vivekamārtaṇḍa, and the longer South Indian recensions printed in the familiar 108-Upaniṣad collection were expanded as late as the 18th century (Bouy 1994). They are valuable witnesses to how Haṭha and Vedānta were combined in the later tradition. Table 1.3 lists the most important; they are treated more fully in Volume 2, Upaniṣad Dīpikā.

Table 1.3. Important Yoga Upaniṣads Upaniṣad Key Teachings Yoga-tattva Up. Four types of Yoga: Mantra, Laya, Haṭha, Rāja Yoga-kuṇḍalinī Up. Kuṇḍalinī; khecarī mudrā (draws on Haṭha texts) Dhyāna-bindu Up. Six-limbed Yoga; meditation on Oṃ; nāḍīs Nāda-bindu Up. Meditation on inner sound (nāda); the mātrās of Oṃ Amṛta-nāda Up. Six-limbed Yoga; Oṃkāra meditation Śāṇḍilya Up. Eight-limbed Yoga; nāḍī description; prāṇāyāma Haṃsa Up. Haṃsa mantra; identification with Brahman Varāha Up. Tattvas; eight-limbed Yoga; nāḍīs

docs.title: 1.5 Yoga in the Epics and Purāṇas
docs.text: The Mahābhārata (composed over several centuries, c. 400 BCE–400 CE) contains extensive teachings on Yoga, much of it earlier than or contemporary with Patañjali’s systematisation; the Rāmāyaṇa is far less concerned with it.

docs.title: 1.5.1 Yoga in the Mahābhārata
docs.text:
Beyond the Bhagavad Gītā, the Mahābhārata contains several other sections devoted to Yoga, including the Mokṣadharma Parva (the section on liberation within the Śānti Parva), which presents extensive teachings on Sāṃkhya-Yoga, the nature of the Self, and various meditative practices. The Anuśāsana Parva contains Bhīṣma’s teachings on dharma, Yoga, and meditation delivered from his bed of arrows.

The epic’s Yoga is closely tied to Sāṃkhya and describes concentration on a single point, breath control and the attainment of supernormal powers; it has been surveyed in detail by Hopkins, Brockington and Bronkhorst (Hopkins 1901; Brockington 2003; Bronkhorst 1993).

Three features of this epic yoga deserve notice, because they differ from both the Upaniṣads and Patañjali. First, Sāṃkhya and Yoga appear as a pair of complementary paths, the one a knowledge of the principles of existence, the other a discipline that confers power; the Mokṣadharma repeatedly asks which is superior, and answers in different ways in different places. Secondly, the yoga described is above all a technique of concentration: the yogin sits still, restrains the senses and the breath, fixes the mind in stages (the epic speaks of dhāraṇās on the elements and on parts of the body), and becomes “like a log”. Some passages describe a fourfold meditation (dhyānayoga) whose stages Bronkhorst has compared with the Buddhist jhānas. Thirdly, the epic’s yogins are powerful. Narratives show them entering the bodies of others — the female ascetic Sulabhā enters the mind of King Janaka in debate, and the sage Vipula enters the body of his teacher’s wife to guard her — and leaving their own bodies at death through the crown of the head, ideas that David Gordon White has traced through later literature (White 2009). Liberation and power were not yet separated; Patañjali’s later warning that the powers are obstacles to samādhi (YS 3.37) is in part a response to this older yoga.

docs.title: 1.5.2 Yogic Themes in the Rāmāyaṇa
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki, while primarily a narrative of Śrī Rāma’s life, contains numerous references to meditative practices, the power of tapas, and the yogic attainments of sages such as Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and Agastya. The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (also called the Mahārāmāyaṇa), traditionally attributed to Vālmīki but in fact a much later Kashmiri work (its earlier form, the Mokṣopāya, is dated to the 10th century CE), is one of the most extensive philosophical texts on Jñāna Yoga, presented as a dialogue between the sage Vasiṣṭha and the young prince Rāma; its teaching on the mind and on yoga is discussed in Chapter 4. Table 1.4 summarises the yogic content of the epics and Purāṇas.

Table 1.4. Yogic Content in the Epics and Purāṇas Text Section Yogic Content Mahābhārata Bhagavad Gītā Karma, Bhakti, Jñāna, Dhyāna Yoga Mahābhārata Mokṣadharma Parva Sāṃkhya-Yoga; meditation; liberation Mahābhārata Anuśāsana Parva Dharma; tapas; yogic disciplines Rāmāyaṇa Bāla Kāṇḍa Sages’ tapas; Viśvāmitra’s austerities Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Six Prakaraṇas Jñāna Yoga; nature of consciousness; māyā Bhāgavata Purāṇa Skandhas 3, 7, 11 Kapila’s Sāṃkhya-Yoga (3); navadhā bhakti (7.5.23); Uddhava Gītā (11) Viṣṇu Purāṇa Book 6 Yoga as union of jīvātman and paramātman Śiva Purāṇa Various Śiva as the great yogin (mahāyogin); meditation; mantra Mārkāṇḍeya Purāṇa Dattātreya and Alarka Yoga practice; obstacles; signs of approaching death Kūrma Purāṇa Īśvaragītā Pāśupata yoga in the frame of Patañjali’s eight limbs Skanda Purāṇa Chs. 174–183 Pāśupata yoga (old Nepalese recension)

docs.title: 1.5.3 Yoga in the Purāṇas
docs.text:
The Purāṇas, composed and recomposed over most of the first millennium CE and later (see Volume 7, Itihāsa–Purāṇa), contain a large and still little-studied body of yoga teaching. It is mostly given in chapters that interrupt the narrative: a god or sage instructs a king or disciple, usually in Patañjali’s eight limbs, but with a personal deity as the object of meditation and with devotion as the setting. The Purāṇas were for centuries the main way in which yoga reached householders, and modern anthologies of yoga’s sources draw heavily on them (Mallinson and Singleton 2017).

Pāśupata yoga. Some of the oldest Purāṇic yoga belongs to the Pāśupatas, the earliest Śaiva ascetic order (Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama). Chapters on Pāśupata yoga in the Vāyu and Liṅga Purāṇas teach the auxiliaries of yoga (five in the Vāyu, Patañjali’s eight in the Liṅga), the obstacles to yoga and the powers it brings. The last ten chapters (174–183) of the old Nepalese recension of the Skanda Purāṇa (probably 6th–7th century) describe a Pāśupata yoga of breath-control, fixation and meditation on Śiva in the heart, with the tongue placed on the palate, a detail that recurs in later Haṭha practice; such passages suggest that some of Haṭha Yoga’s techniques have roots in pre-Tantric Śaiva asceticism. The Īśvaragītā, eleven chapters that open the second part of the Kūrma Purāṇa, is a Śaiva counterpart to the Bhagavad Gītā in which Śiva teaches a Pāśupata yoga built on Patañjali’s eight limbs (Nicholson 2014).

Dattātreya. In the Mārkāṇḍeya Purāṇa the sage Dattātreya teaches yoga to King Alarka: breath-control and the other auxiliaries, the dangers and obstacles that beset the yogin, the signs by which he can foresee his death, and the practice of leaving the body. This episode helped make Dattātreya the patron deity of yogis, the “lord of yoga” to whom the Vaiṣṇava Dattātreyayogaśāstra (Chapter 7) and later the Nāths and Mahānubhāvas looked back (Rigopoulos 1998).

Vaiṣṇava yoga. In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (book 6) King Keśidhvaja teaches his kinsman Khāṇḍikya a yoga defined as the joining of the mind to brahman; its meditation is on the visible form of Viṣṇu, called the “auspicious support” (śubhāśraya), on which the mind rests before passing to the formless. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa goes further. Kapila’s teaching to his mother Devahūti (3.28) leads the yogin through the eight limbs to a meditation that dwells on Viṣṇu’s body limb by limb, from the feet to the smiling face; in the eleventh book Kṛṣṇa teaches Uddhava the techniques of meditation, lists eighteen yogic powers and declares them distractions from devotion (11.15), and names three yogas — of knowledge, of action and of devotion (11.20) — a scheme that anticipates the modern classification of the paths of yoga (Section 1.9). Here yoga is subordinated to bhakti: the powers are worthless, meditation is a form of loving remembrance, and liberation is service of the Lord.

Later, encyclopaedic Purāṇas such as the Agni and Garuḍa include compact summaries of eight-limbed yoga alongside their sections on ritual, medicine and law. Taken together, the Purāṇas show that Patañjali’s scheme of eight limbs was widely known in the first millennium even where his metaphysics was not: the limbs were kept, but the goal became union with, or service of, a personal god.

docs.title: 1.6 The Concept of the Guru in Yoga
docs.text:
Almost every Yoga lineage has been transmitted from teacher to disciple (guru–śiṣya), and the texts give the teacher an authority that is hard to overstate. A widely recited verse, found in the Guru Gītā and in many devotional collections, expresses the exalted view of the teacher:

Popular verse in praise of the Guru

gurur brahmā gurur viṣṇur gurur devo maheśvaraḥ guruḥ sākṣāt paraṃ brahma tasmai śrīgurave namaḥ The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is Lord Maheśvara (Śiva). The Guru is verily the Supreme Brahman. Salutations to that glorious Guru.

The tradition holds that the highest truths of Yoga cannot be learned from books alone but must be received from a teacher who has travelled the path. The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad declares: tad-vijñānārthaṃ sa gurum evābhigacchet samit-pāṇiḥ śrotriyaṃ brahma-niṣṭham — “To know That (Brahman), one should approach a Guru, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the scriptures and established in Brahman” (1.2.12). The two qualities named here, learning in the Veda (śrotriya) and establishment in Brahman (brahmaniṣṭha), head the lists of a teacher’s qualifications in later Vedāntic manuals such as the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (33), which add freedom from desire, blamelessness, calm and compassion.

The same tradition that exalts the guru also places great power in the guru’s hands. Modern Yoga has seen serious abuses of that power (see Chapter 11); classical texts themselves insist that the teacher be tested for learning and conduct before being accepted.

docs.title: 1.7 Yoga and Allied Disciplines
docs.text: Yoga has always borrowed from, and lent to, neighbouring disciplines of the Bhāratīya knowledge system (jñāna paramparā). The closest are Sāṃkhya, which supplied Patañjala Yoga with its metaphysics; Vedānta, which absorbed yoga and argued with it (Chapter 4); Tantra, from which Haṭha Yoga took its subtle body (Chapters 5–6); and Āyurveda. Each has its own volume in this series: Volume 3 on the darśanas, Volume 6 on Tantra and Volume 13 on Āyurveda. Music theory also took over the yogic doctrine of inner sound (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 1.7.1 Yoga and Āyurveda
docs.text: Yoga and Āyurveda share a common vocabulary of breath, digestion (agni) and the humours (doṣa), and Haṭha texts claim that particular practices cure diseases of vāta, pitta and kapha. Historically, however, the two developed largely independently. The classical compendia of Caraka and Suśruta say little about yogic technique, with one notable exception: towards the end of the first chapter of the Carakasaṃhitā’s section on the embodied person (Śārīrasthāna), yoga and liberation (mokṣa) are presented as the means by which all painful sensations cease, the one temporarily and the other for ever, and the yogin’s eight powers are listed. Dominik Wujastyk has shown that this passage teaches a yoga of mindfulness (smṛti) close to early Buddhist and Sāṃkhya ideas, and that it is among the oldest systematic accounts of yoga in Sanskrit (Wujastyk 2012). The systematic pairing of āsana and prāṇāyāma with an individual’s constitution (prakṛti) — cooling breaths for a pitta type, vigorous postures for kapha, and so on — is a modern development, popularised in books such as David Frawley’s Yoga and Ayurveda (Frawley 1999); it is not a classical prescription.

docs.title: 1.7.2 Yoga and Sāṃkhya
docs.text:
Yoga is traditionally paired with Sāṃkhya as one of the six darśanas. While Sāṃkhya provides the theoretical framework — the enumeration of the twenty-five tattvas (principles) from Puruṣa and Prakṛti through to the five gross elements — Yoga provides the practical methodology for realising the truth that Sāṃkhya describes. The Bhagavad Gītā (5.5) puts it succinctly: ekaṃ sāṃkhyaṃ ca yogaṃ ca yaḥ paśyati sa paśyati — “He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, truly sees.” (In the Gītā these words mean the paths of knowledge and of disciplined action rather than the later classical schools.)

Scholarly Note: The Sāṃkhya-Yoga Relationship

The philosophical relationship between Sāṃkhya and Yoga has been a subject of extensive scholarly discussion. While the classical Sāṃkhya of Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s Sāṃkhya Kārikā is technically nirīśvara (atheistic, without a concept of God), Patañjali’s Yoga system is seśvara (theistic, including the concept of īśvara). Despite this difference, the two systems share the same cosmological framework of Puruṣa and Prakṛti, the same analysis of the guṇas, and the same ultimate goal of kaivalya (liberation through discrimination).

docs.title: 1.8 The Concept of Consciousness in Yoga
docs.text: One of the most distinctive contributions of the Upaniṣadic and yogic traditions is their detailed mapping of states of consciousness, including dream, deep sleep and meditative absorption.

docs.title: 1.8.1 The Four States of Consciousness (Avasthā Catuṣṭaya)
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, one of the shortest yet most philosophically dense of all Upaniṣads, describes four states of consciousness (Table 1.5):

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 7

nāntaḥ-prajñaṃ na bahiṣ-prajñaṃ nobhayataḥ-prajñaṃ na prajñāna-ghanaṃ na prajñaṃ nāprajñam adṛṣṭam avyavahāryam agrāhyam alakṣaṇam acintyam avyapadeśyam ekātma-pratyaya-sāraṃ prapañcopaśamaṃ śāntaṃ śivam advaitam caturthaṃ manyante sa ātmā sa vijñeyaḥ Not inward-turned consciousness, not outward-turned consciousness, not both together, not a mass of consciousness, not consciousness and not unconsciousness. It is unseen, beyond empirical dealings, ungraspable, without marks, unthinkable, indescribable. Its essence is the experience of its own Self. It is the cessation of the phenomenal world — peaceful, auspicious, non-dual. That is the Fourth (Turīya). That is the Ātman. That is to be known.

Table 1.5. The Four States of Consciousness (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, with the later Vedāntic three bodies) State Sanskrit Oṃ Sound Body Description Waking Jāgarita A Sthūla Outward-turned awareness; sense perception Dream Svapna U Sūkṣma Inward-turned awareness; subtle impressions Deep Sleep Suṣupti M Kāraṇa Undifferentiated consciousness; bliss The Fourth Turīya Silence Beyond Pure awareness; the Ātman itself

docs.title: 1.8.2 Modern Neuroscience: An Analogy, Not a Confirmation
docs.text: It is sometimes claimed that the Upaniṣadic states correspond to EEG frequency bands (beta for waking, alpha and theta for meditation, gamma for turīya). No such correspondence has been established, and the Upaniṣads should not be read as anticipating neuroscience. What can be said is more modest. Laboratory studies show that meditation alters measurable brain activity; for example, Lutz and colleagues reported unusually high-amplitude gamma-band synchrony in long-term Tibetan Buddhist practitioners during a compassion meditation (Lutz et al. 2004). Whether such findings bear on the metaphysical claims of Vedānta or Yoga is a philosophical question that laboratory data cannot settle.

docs.title: 1.9 The Principal Streams of Yoga
docs.text:
Modern Hindu teaching speaks of several paths (mārga) of Yoga, each suited to a particular temperament. The best-known scheme, of four yogas — Rāja, Karma, Bhakti and Jñāna — is Vivekānanda’s: he lectured and published on each of them in the 1890s, and his books made the classification standard (De Michelis 2004). It had precedents. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa already names three yogas of knowledge, action and devotion (11.20; Section 1.5.3), and the medieval yoga texts arranged four others — Mantra, Laya, Haṭha and Rāja — in a hierarchy (Chapter 7). Modern teaching presents all of them as tributaries of one river; historically they arose in different milieux and were often rivals. Table 1.6 summarises the key text, faculty and method that modern accounts attach to each.

Table 1.6. The Principal Paths of Yoga as Classified in Modern Teaching Path Key Text Faculty Method Rāja Yoga Yoga Sūtras Mind (manas) Eight limbs; mental discipline Haṭha Yoga HYP, GS, ŚS Body (śarīra) Āsana, prāṇāyāma, mudrā, bandha Karma Yoga Bhagavad Gītā Will (saṃkalpa) Selfless action; niṣkāma karma Bhakti Yoga BG; NBS Heart (hṛdaya) Devotion; surrender; love Jñāna Yoga Upaniṣads; VS Intellect (buddhi) Inquiry; discrimination; knowledge Kuṇḍalinī Yoga Tantric texts Energy (prāṇa) Cakra activation; kuṇḍalinī awakening Mantra Yoga Tantra; Veda Sound (nāda) Japa; sacred syllables Tantra Yoga Āgamas Totality Integration of all faculties

Abbreviations as in the list of abbreviations at the front of the volume.

docs.title: 1.10 Key Texts of the Yoga Tradition
docs.text: The texts on which this volume draws fall into four broad layers, whose dates are set out in the Chronology at the end of the book. The first is Vedic: the Ṛgveda’s references to tapas and to ecstatic ascetics, and the Upaniṣads — Kaṭha, Śvetāśvatara, Maitrī, Māṇḍūkya — in which a method of meditation is first described. The second is classical: Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra with its Bhāṣya and the long line of commentaries that runs from the Vivaraṇa and Vācaspati Miśra to Vijñānabhikṣu (Chapter 2), together with the Bhagavad Gītā and the yoga chapters of the epic and the Purāṇas. The third is Tantric: the Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava and Buddhist scriptures in which the subtle body was mapped (Chapters 5–6). The fourth is the Haṭha corpus, from the eleventh-century Amṛtasiddhi and the Dattātreyayogaśāstra (c. 1200) through the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā (c. 1450) to the eighteenth-century Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati (Chapter 7). Alongside these run the devotional literature — the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and the Nārada and Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtras — and, from the twelfth century, a growing body of yoga in the regional languages, in Persian and in Arabic.

docs.title: 1.11 The Philosophical Framework of Yoga
docs.text: As noted in Section 1.7, Patañjala Yoga takes its metaphysics largely from Sāṃkhya. This section sets out that framework and the Upaniṣadic model of the five sheaths, both of which recur throughout the volume.

docs.title: 1.11.1 The Sāṃkhya-Yoga Framework
docs.text:
Figure 1.2. The twenty-five tattvas of the Sāṃkhya-Yoga framework. Puruṣa, pure consciousness, stands apart from Prakṛti, which is composed of the three guṇas and evolves into buddhi and then ahaṃkāra; following Sāṃkhya Kārikā 25, the sāttvika aspect of ahaṃkāra yields mind and the ten senses, the tāmasa aspect the subtle elements, from which the gross elements arise, and rajas activates both.

The Sāṃkhya system posits two fundamental realities (Figure 1.2): puruṣa, consciousness, the eternal and unchanging witness; and prakṛti, nature, the dynamic principle composed of the three guṇas — sattva (illumination), rajas (activity) and tamas (inertia). Bondage (bandha) arises from the confusion of Puruṣa with Prakṛti — the mistaken identification of the Self with the body-mind complex. Liberation (kaivalya) is the discriminative realisation (viveka-khyāti) that Puruṣa is eternally free and distinct from Prakṛti. Yoga is the practical means to achieve this realisation.

docs.title: 1.11.2 The Pañca Kośa Model
docs.text:
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1–5) describes the human being as five concentric sheaths (kośas), from the gross to the most subtle (Figure 1.3; Table 1.7). Advaita Vedānta later used the scheme as a method of discrimination, setting each sheath aside in turn as “not the self”; modern teachers, as in the third column of the table, match the sheaths to the limbs of yoga.

Figure 1.3. The Pañca Kośa Model — Five Sheaths of the Human Being (Taittirīya Upaniṣad). Table 1.7. The Pañca Kośa (Five Sheaths), with the Yoga Practices Matched to Them in Modern Teaching Kośa English Yoga Practice Description Annamaya Food sheath Āsana, Ṣaṭkarma Physical body nourished by food Prāṇamaya Vital sheath Prāṇāyāma Energy body; the five prāṇas Manomaya Mental sheath Pratyāhāra Mind and emotions Vijñānamaya Wisdom sheath Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna Discriminative intellect Ānandamaya Bliss sheath Samādhi Causal body; deep bliss

docs.title: 1.12 Yoga as a Living Tradition
docs.text:
What distinguishes Yoga from a mere philosophical system or historical curiosity is that it remains a living tradition. Millions of practitioners across the globe continue to practise it, although most modern practice — centred on postures and largely pursued for health — differs considerably from the meditative and renunciant Yoga of the classical texts (Chapter 11).

In December 2014 the United Nations General Assembly, on India’s initiative, declared 21 June the International Day of Yoga. Clinical research suggests that yoga can modestly help with conditions such as chronic low-back pain and anxiety, but the evidence is uneven in quality and many popular health claims remain unproven (see Section 11.11).

In the classical sources, however, the aim of Yoga lies beyond health and well-being: it is liberation, whether understood as the kaivalya of Sāṃkhya-Yoga, the mokṣa of Vedānta or the nirvāṇa of the Buddhists.

docs.title: 1.13 Structure of This Volume
docs.text: The chapters follow the currents of yoga roughly in the order in which they arose, so that each technique is met after the ideas from which it grew. Chapter 2 treats Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra: its four parts, its eight limbs, its theory of mind and the commentators who interpreted it for fifteen centuries. Chapter 3 turns to the Gītā’s yogas of action and devotion and to their later history, and Chapter 4 asks how the Advaita Vedāntins, for whom liberation came by knowledge alone, used and criticised yoga. Chapters 5 and 6 describe the yoga of the Tantras and the subtle body of channels, centres and kuṇḍalinī that the Tantras devised. Chapter 7 follows Haṭha Yoga, which inherited that body, from the Amṛtasiddhi to the Mysore court, together with the ascetic orders that carried it and its life in Tamil, Marathi, Persian and the Sikh scriptures. Chapters 8 to 10 take up three practices that run through all these traditions: breath-control, meditation (with its Buddhist and Jain forms) and the yogas of mantra, dissolution and inner sound. Chapter 11 traces modern yoga from Vivekānanda to the International Day of Yoga, including its politics, its scandals and the clinical evidence. A chronology, a glossary and a select bibliography close the volume.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra and the Eight Limbs
docs.text:
Traditional invocation to Patañjali (a late verse, found in an 18th-century work by Śivarāma)

yogena cittasya padena vācāṃ malaṃ śarīrasya ca vaidyakena yo'pākarot taṃ pravaraṃ munīnāṃ patañjaliṃ prāñjalir ānato'smi I bow with folded hands to Patañjali, the foremost among sages, who removed impurities of the mind through Yoga, of speech through Grammar, and of the body through Medicine.

docs.title: 2.1 Patañjali and His Work
docs.text:
Patañjali did not invent Yoga. He systematised existing yogic teachings — Brahmanical, and in part Buddhist in vocabulary — into a compact work of 195 or 196 aphorisms (sūtras), whose terseness invites comparison with Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī. Later tradition, in the invocation above, made him the author of three works that purify mind, speech and body: the Yoga Sūtra, the Mahābhāṣya on grammar and a lost medical treatise. Modern scholarship does not accept this attribution.

The dating of Patañjali has long been debated. The identification of the author of the Yoga Sūtras with Patañjali the grammarian (c. 150 BCE) would place him in the 2nd century BCE, but most modern scholars reject it on grounds of language and doctrine. Philipp Maas, who produced the first critical edition of the work’s first chapter (Maas 2006), has shown from the manuscript tradition that the sūtras and the Bhāṣya ascribed to “Vyāsa” were transmitted as one work, the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, which he dates to c. 325–425 CE; he argues that Patañjali compiled the sūtras and wrote the explanatory prose himself (Maas 2013). Not all scholars accept single authorship, but a date around the 4th–5th century CE for the work in its present form is now widely accepted. The text shows considerable familiarity with Sarvāstivāda and Yogācāra Buddhist ideas, and Karen O’Brien-Kop has argued that “classical” Yoga is best read as one participant in a shared Brahmanical and Buddhist discourse of meditation rather than as a self-contained system (Bryant 2009; White 2014; O’Brien-Kop 2021).

docs.title: 2.2 Structure of the Yoga Sūtras
docs.text:
The sūtras are divided into four chapters (pādas), each addressing a distinct aspect of the yogic path. (The count of 55 or 56 sūtras in the third chapter varies between editions; sūtra numbers cited below follow the common numbering of Woods’s translation (Woods 1914).) Table 2.1 gives the subject of each pāda. This chapter follows the four parts in turn, but treats the eight limbs, which run from the end of the second part into the third, together (Section 2.5).

Table 2.1. The Four Pādas of the Yoga Sūtras Pāda Name Sūtras Subject Matter I Samādhi Pāda 51 Nature of Yoga; states of samādhi; obstacles II Sādhana Pāda 55 Practice; kleśas; Kriyā Yoga; first five limbs III Vibhūti Pāda 56 Supernatural powers (siddhis); last three limbs IV Kaivalya Pāda 34 Absolute liberation; nature of consciousness

docs.title: 2.3 Pāda I: Samādhi Pāda — The Chapter on Absorption
docs.text: Later commentators held that the first chapter is addressed to the student who is already advanced in practice. It defines Yoga, describes the modifications of the mind, names the obstacles and their remedies, and presents the stages of samādhi.

docs.title: 2.3.1 The Opening Sūtras: Definition of Yoga
docs.text:
Sūtra 1.1

atha yogānuśāsanam Now begins the authoritative instruction on Yoga.

Vyāsa’s Bhāṣya explains that atha (“now”) marks the beginning of a topic (adhikāra), and glosses the word yoga as concentration (samādhi).

Sūtra 1.2 — The Definition

yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind-stuff.

This is the defining sūtra (lakṣaṇa sūtra). Citta is the whole mental apparatus — in the commentators’ terms, the Sāṃkhya mind, intellect and ego-sense together (Section 2.9); its vṛttis are its fluctuations or modifications; nirodha is their cessation or restraint.

Sūtra 1.3 — The Result

tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam Then the Seer abides in its own true nature.

When the fluctuations of the mind cease, the Puruṣa (the Seer, draṣṭā) rests in its own nature; when they do not, it seems to take on their form (vṛtti-sārūpyam itaratra, 1.4).

docs.title: 2.3.2 The Five Vṛttis
docs.text:
Sūtra 1.5–1.6

vṛttayaḥ pañcatayyaḥ kliṣṭākliṣṭāḥ pramāṇa-viparyaya-vikalpa-nidrā-smṛtayaḥ The fluctuations are fivefold, and may be painful (kliṣṭa) or non-painful (akliṣṭa). They are: valid cognition, error, imagination, sleep, and memory.

Each of the five may be painful or not; Table 2.2 gives the sūtra that defines each.

Table 2.2. The Five Vṛttis and Their Characteristics Vṛtti English Description Sūtra Pramāṇa Valid cognition Correct knowledge through perception, inference, or testimony 1.7 Viparyaya Error Misconception; knowledge not based on the real form of the object 1.8 Vikalpa Imagination Verbal cognition without a corresponding object 1.9 Nidrā Sleep The modification based on the absence of content 1.10 Smṛti Memory Retention of experienced objects 1.11

docs.title: 2.3.3 Abhyāsa and Vairāgya
docs.text:
Sūtra 1.12

abhyāsa-vairāgyābhyāṃ tan-nirodhaḥ The cessation of the fluctuations is achieved through practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya).

Sūtra 1.13–1.14

tatra sthitau yatno'bhyāsaḥ sa tu dīrgha-kāla-nairantarya-satkārāsevito dṛḍha-bhūmiḥ Of these, abhyāsa is the effort to maintain steadiness. That practice becomes firmly grounded when pursued for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion.

The three conditions of firm practice — long duration (dīrgha-kāla), continuity (nairantarya) and care or reverence (satkāra) — are the nearest the sūtras come to a programme of training. Dispassion is defined next (1.15–1.16): the lower kind is mastery over craving for things seen or heard of; the higher (para-vairāgya) is indifference even to the qualities of nature, which comes from knowledge of the Puruṣa.

docs.title: 2.3.4 Īśvara Praṇidhāna
docs.text:
One of the most distinctive features of Patañjali’s Yoga, compared with classical Sāṃkhya, is the inclusion of Īśvara (the Lord) as a special Puruṣa. Īśvara is not a creator; he is a self who has never been bound and who serves as teacher and object of meditation:

Sūtras 1.23–1.27

īśvara-praṇidhānād vā kleśa-karma-vipākāśayair aparāmṛṣṭaḥ puruṣa-viśeṣa īśvaraḥ tatra niratiśayaṃ sarva-jña-bījam pūrveṣām api guruḥ kālenānavacchedāt tasya vācakaḥ praṇavaḥ Or, (samādhi is attained) by devotion to Īśvara. Īśvara is a special Puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, actions, results, or latent impressions. In Him is the unsurpassed seed of omniscience. He is the Guru even of the ancients, being not limited by time. His designator (name) is the Praṇava (Oṃ).

The next sūtra prescribes the repetition of this syllable together with contemplation of its meaning (1.28; Chapter 10).

docs.title: 2.3.5 The Obstacles and Their Remedies
docs.text:
The first chapter also analyses what stands in the way of practice:

Sūtra 1.30

vyādhi-styāna-saṃśaya-pramādālāsyāvirati- bhrānti-darśanālabdha-bhūmikatvānavasthitatvāni citta-vikṣepās te'ntarāyāḥ Disease, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, worldliness, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability — these are the distractions of the mind that are the obstacles.

Pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs and irregular breathing accompany these distractions (1.31). Table 2.3 gives Vyāsa’s explanation of each obstacle.

Table 2.3. The Nine Obstacles (Antarāyas), YS 1.30 Obstacle English Description (following Vyāsa) Vyādhi Disease Imbalance of the bodily humours, fluids and senses Styāna Dullness Mental inertia; unwillingness to act Saṃśaya Doubt Wavering between alternatives Pramāda Carelessness Failure to cultivate the means to samādhi Ālasya Laziness Heaviness of body and mind Avirati Worldliness Craving for sense objects Bhrānti-darśana False perception Mistaken understanding Alabdha-bhūmikatva Non-attainment Failure to reach a stage of concentration Anavasthitatva Instability Inability to hold an attained stage

Patañjali’s own remedy is practice on a single principle (eka-tattvābhyāsa, 1.32). He then offers a series of alternatives for steadying the mind: cultivating friendliness, compassion, joy and equanimity towards the happy, the suffering, the virtuous and the wicked (1.33, discussed as a meditation practice in Chapter 9); the expulsion and retention of breath (1.34); engagement of the mind with a subtle sense-experience (1.35); a luminous state free of sorrow (1.36); a mind free from passion, such as that of a saint (1.37); the knowledge of dream or deep sleep (1.38); and, finally, meditation on any object one likes (1.39). The list is notably open: no single technique is required, and a range of supports is offered for people of different temperaments.

docs.title: 2.3.6 The Stages of Samādhi
docs.text:
This is the book’s one full treatment of the stages of samādhi; the chapters on Haṭha Yoga and on meditation refer back to it. Patañjali distinguishes two kinds of absorption. Cognitive (samprajñāta) absorption is accompanied by gross thought (vitarka), subtle reflection (vicāra), bliss (ānanda) and the bare sense “I am” (asmitā) (1.17); the other kind, reached through supreme dispassion (para-vairāgya, 1.16) and the practice of the idea of cessation, retains only latent impressions (1.18).

Sūtras 1.41–1.51 analyse cognitive absorption as a series of “coalescences” (samāpatti) of the mind with its object, which become progressively simpler. In savitarka absorption the object is still mixed with its name and with the idea of it (1.42); when memory is purified, the object alone shines forth (nirvitarka, 1.43). The same two steps are then repeated with subtle objects (savicāra, nirvicāra, 1.44). All of these are “with seed” (sabīja, 1.46). At the highest of them the mind becomes so clear that its insight is called “truth-bearing” (ṛtaṃbharā prajñā, 1.48), and the impression left by that insight blocks all other impressions (1.50). When even this impression is stopped, the absorption is “seedless” (nirbīja, 1.51). The commentators, from Vyāsa onwards, built these sūtras into a ladder of six cognitive stages leading to the non-cognitive state; Vācaspati Miśra’s systematisation of that ladder is the one usually taught today (Figure 2.1; Table 2.4). The final stage before liberation, the “cloud of dharma” (dharmamegha), is described in the fourth chapter (Section 2.7).

Figure 2.1. Classification of Samādhi in Patañjali’s Yoga System. All cognitive (samprajñāta) samādhis are “with seed” (1.46); the seedless state is the cessation of even the final impression (1.51). The finer subdivision and the placement of dharmamegha follow the commentators. Table 2.4. Stages of Samādhi as Systematised by the Commentators Stage Type Object Characteristics Savitarka Cognitive Gross Absorption with name, form, and knowledge mixed Nirvitarka Cognitive Gross Only the object’s essential nature shines Savicāra Cognitive Subtle Absorption on subtle elements with reflection Nirvicāra Cognitive Subtle Truth-bearing insight (ṛtaṃbharā prajñā) Sānanda Cognitive Sattvic joy Absorption in pure bliss Sāsmitā Cognitive Pure ego Only the sense of “I am” remains Asamprajñāta Non-cognitive None Cessation of all mental activity; seedless

docs.title: 2.4 Pāda II: Sādhana Pāda — The Chapter on Practice
docs.text: According to the commentators, the second chapter is addressed to the student of intermediate qualification who requires practical guidance. It introduces Kriyā Yoga, analyses the causes of suffering (kleśas), and begins the account of the eight limbs.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Kriyā Yoga: The Yoga of Action
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.1

tapaḥ-svādhyāyeśvara-praṇidhānāni kriyā-yogaḥ Austerity (tapas), self-study (svādhyāya), and surrender to Īśvara (īśvara-praṇidhāna) constitute Kriyā Yoga.

Kriyā Yoga is practised, the next sūtra says, to cultivate samādhi and to weaken the afflictions (2.2). The same three practices reappear as the last three observances (niyama) of the eight-limbed path (Section 2.5.2), and the commentators read Kriyā Yoga as the yoga of those not yet fit for the higher practices of the first chapter.

docs.title: 2.4.2 The Five Kleśas (Afflictions)
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.3

avidyāsmitā-rāga-dveṣābhiniveśāḥ kleśāḥ The afflictions are: ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life.

Table 2.5 summarises the five.

Table 2.5. The Pañca Kleśas (Five Afflictions) Kleśa English Description Sūtra Avidyā Ignorance Mistaking the non-eternal for eternal, impure for pure, painful for pleasant, non-Self for Self 2.5 Asmitā Egoism Identification of the Seer with the instrument of seeing 2.6 Rāga Attachment Clinging to pleasure 2.7 Dveṣa Aversion Recoiling from pain 2.8 Abhiniveśa Fear of death Clinging to life, present even in the wise 2.9

Sūtra 2.4 — Avidyā as the Root

avidyā kṣetram uttareṣāṃ prasupta-tanu-vicchinnōdārāṇām Ignorance is the field for the others, whether they be dormant, attenuated, alternating, or fully active.

Because ignorance is the field in which the others grow, the analysis has a single point of attack. Egoism arises because the instrument of seeing is mistaken for the seer; attachment and aversion follow the pleasant and the painful; and the fear of death comes from identifying the self with the mortal body. Remove ignorance, and the other afflictions lose their ground. The means of removing it is named a little later:

Sūtra 2.26

viveka-khyātir aviplavā hānopāyaḥ The means of liberation (hāna-upāya) is unbroken discriminative discernment (viveka-khyāti).

Viveka-khyāti is not intellectual analysis but a direct perception of the difference between the Seer (Puruṣa) and the seen (Prakṛti), the fruit of the truth-bearing insight of the higher samādhis. The eight limbs, to which the sūtras now turn, are presented as the practice that destroys impurity until this discernment shines forth (2.28).

docs.title: 2.5 The Eight Limbs (YS 2.28–3.8)
docs.text:
Yoga Sūtra 2.29

yama-niyamāsana-prāṇāyāma-pratyāhāra-dhāraṇā-dhyāna-samādhayo'ṣṭāv aṅgāni Restraint, observance, posture, breath regulation, sense withdrawal, concentration, meditation, and absorption — these are the eight limbs.

The aṣṭāṅga or eight-limbed yoga is the best-known framework of yogic practice in the Brahmanical tradition, and the one most often taken as normative in modern times. Aṅga means “limb” or “auxiliary”, not “step”: the eight are parts of a single discipline, and the ethical limbs are meant to be kept throughout. Patañjali himself divides them into two groups (YS 3.7–3.8). The first five are “external” (bahiraṅga); the last three are “internal” (antaraṅga), though they are in turn external in relation to seedless samādhi (Figure 2.2). B.K.S. Iyengar’s image of the limbs as the parts of a tree, from the root of yama to the fruit of samādhi, makes the same point for modern readers (Iyengar 1988).

Figure 2.2. The Eight Limbs of Aṣṭāṅga Yoga, from external discipline to inner absorption, with Patañjali’s division into external and internal limbs (YS 3.7–3.8).

docs.title: 2.5.1 Yama: The Restraints
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.30

ahiṃsā-satyāsteya-brahmacaryāparigrahā yamāḥ Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence, and non-possessiveness are the restraints.

When the restraints are kept without limitation of birth, place, time or circumstance, Patañjali calls them the “great vow” (mahāvrata, 2.31); Vyāsa’s example of a limited vow is the fisherman who harms only fish. Ahiṃsā comes first, and Vyāsa makes the others depend on it. He defines it as sarvathā sarvadā sarvabhūtānām anabhidrohaḥ, “the absence of injurious intent towards all living beings, in every way, at all times”, and adds that the other restraints and observances are practised to perfect it. Satya is speech and thought that accord with what has been seen, inferred or heard, spoken for the good of others; asteya is the absence of the wish to take what belongs to another; aparigraha is freedom from acquisitiveness.

Brahmacarya originally meant the life of a Vedic student (“one who moves in brahman”, that is, in Vedic study), which required chastity. In the Yoga Sūtra it means sexual continence: Vyāsa defines it as restraint of the sexual organ together with the other senses, and Patañjali was writing for renunciants. The Yoga Upaniṣads (for example the Śāṇḍilya) extend the definition to thought and word, and the Haṭha texts add a physiological reason, the preservation of semen (bindu). For the householder Dharmaśāstra prescribes not celibacy but marital fidelity. Many modern teachers reinterpret brahmacarya as moderation in general; that is a reading for lay practitioners, distinct from the ascetic meaning of the classical sources.

The sūtras then state what each restraint brings when it is firmly established (2.35–2.39): hostility ceases in the yogin’s presence; his words come true; jewels present themselves to him; he gains vigour (vīrya); and he knows the circumstances of his births. These are claims of the tradition; Vyāsa illustrates the first with natural enemies living peacefully near the sage.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Niyama: The Observances
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.32

śauca-saṃtoṣa-tapaḥ-svādhyāyeśvara-praṇidhānāni niyamāḥ Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and surrender to the Lord are the observances.

Where the restraints govern the yogin’s dealings with others, the observances govern his own discipline. Śauca is both external purity, of the body and of food, and internal purity of mind; the first is said to bring disgust for one’s own body and disinclination for contact with others, the second cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses and fitness for the vision of the self (2.40–2.41). Santoṣa, contentment, yields unsurpassed happiness (2.42). Tapas, literally “heat”, is the endurance of the pairs of opposites — heat and cold, hunger and thirst — by which impurity is destroyed and the body and senses are perfected (2.43); the Bhagavad Gītā (17.14–16) distinguishes austerity of body, of speech and of mind. Svādhyāya is, for Vyāsa, the study of texts that lead to liberation or the repetition of Oṃ, and it brings contact with one’s chosen deity (2.44); the modern gloss “study of the self” extends the etymology (sva, “own”) rather than the classical meaning. Īśvara-praṇidhāna is, in Vyāsa’s words, the offering of all actions to the supreme teacher, and through it samādhi is perfected (2.45).

docs.title: 2.5.3 Āsana: The Seat
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.46

sthira-sukham āsanam The posture should be steady and comfortable.

The word āsana literally means “seat” (from ās, “to sit”). In the Yoga Sūtra it is the seated posture in which the yogin remains for long periods of breath-control and meditation. Vyāsa names about a dozen such seats (lotus, hero, auspicious, staff and others); none is a standing or athletic posture (Figure 2.3). Perfection in posture comes from relaxing effort and from absorption in the infinite (2.47), and then the yogin is no longer troubled by the pairs of opposites (2.48). The very different āsana of Haṭha Yoga, and the long history by which “seat” became “posture”, are traced in Chapter 7.

Figure 2.3. Ascetics in yogic and austere postures, including seated lotus-type postures; South Indian gouache, c. 1820 (Musée Guimet, Paris). Photo: Jean-Pierre Dalbéra, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 2.5.4 Prāṇāyāma: Regulation of the Breath
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.49

tasmin sati śvāsa-praśvāsayor gati-vicchedaḥ prāṇāyāmaḥ That (āsana) being established, prāṇāyāma is the interruption of the flow of inhalation and exhalation.

For Patañjali, prāṇāyāma is not a set of breathing exercises but the stopping of breath movement. Sūtra 2.50 distinguishes three forms of this cessation, each to be measured by place, time and number until it becomes “long and subtle”; 2.51 adds a “fourth” that goes beyond the external and internal spheres; and 2.52–2.53 state its fruits: the covering of the inner light wears away and the mind becomes fit for concentration. These sūtras, Vyāsa’s explanation of them and the very different techniques of Haṭha Yoga are discussed in Chapter 8 (Section 8.9).

docs.title: 2.5.5 Pratyāhāra: Withdrawal of the Senses
docs.text:
Sūtra 2.54

sva-viṣayāsaṃprayoge citta-svarūpānukāra ivendriyāṇāṃ pratyāhāraḥ Pratyāhāra is, as it were, the imitation by the senses of the mind’s own nature, when they withdraw from their objects.

Pratyāhāra is the hinge between the external and the internal limbs. Vyāsa compares the senses to bees that rise and settle with their king: when the mind is restrained, the senses follow it. The older image is the tortoise withdrawing its limbs into its shell (Bhagavad Gītā 2.58). From withdrawal comes supreme mastery over the senses (tataḥ paramā vaśyatendriyāṇām, 2.55). It is the limb least discussed in modern posture practice. Some Brahmanical and Haṭha yoga texts, such as the Yogayājñavalkya, give it a technical sense of their own, as the withdrawal of the breath from a series of vital points in the body.

docs.title: 2.5.6 Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna and Samādhi
docs.text:
The third chapter of the sūtras opens by defining the three internal limbs:

Sūtras 3.1–3.3

deśa-bandhaś cittasya dhāraṇā tatra pratyayaikatānatā dhyānam tad evārtha-mātra-nirbhāsaṃ svarūpa-śūnyam iva samādhiḥ Dhāraṇā is the binding of the mind to a single location. Dhyāna is the unbroken flow of cognition towards that object. When that same (meditation) shines forth as the object alone, as if devoid of its own form — that is Samādhi.

In dhāraṇā the mind, withdrawn from external objects, is fixed on a chosen place (deśa). Vyāsa lists places in the body — the navel circle, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose and the tip of the tongue — and external objects; later traditions added images of the deity, flames, yantras and mantras. The mind still wanders and must be brought back. When the stream of attention (pratyaya) towards the object becomes continuous (ekatānatā), dhāraṇā has become dhyāna; later commentators compare it to oil poured in an unbroken stream from one vessel to another. The difference between the two is one of degree. (Some later Haṭha texts and Yoga Upaniṣads quantify it, making one unit of dhyāna equal to twelve of dhāraṇā; this is not found in Patañjali or Vyāsa.) In samādhi, finally, the object alone shines forth, and the mind is so absorbed in it that it seems empty of its own form. The texts do not describe this as unconsciousness or blankness: the sūtras compare the purified mind to a flawless jewel that takes on the colour of whatever is placed beside it (1.41), and the higher samādhis are states of heightened clarity in which the truth-bearing insight arises (Section 2.3.6). Meditation as a practice, with its objects and its Buddhist and Jain forms, is the subject of Chapter 9.

docs.title: 2.5.7 Saṃyama
docs.text:
Sūtras 3.4–3.5

trayam ekatra saṃyamaḥ taj-jayāt prajñālokaḥ The three (dhāraṇā, dhyāna, samādhi) together form Saṃyama. By mastery of saṃyama, the light of wisdom dawns.

Practised together on a single object, the three internal limbs are called saṃyama. In Patañjali’s account saṃyama is the yogin’s instrument of knowledge: directed at any object, gross or subtle, it is said to reveal that object completely, and the powers of the third chapter arise from applying it to different objects (Section 2.6).

docs.title: 2.5.8 Other Schemes of Limbs
docs.text:
The eight-limbed system of Patañjali is not the only multi-limbed classification of Yoga in the Bhāratīya tradition. Several other texts present alternative schemes (Table 2.6).

Table 2.6. Comparative Analysis of Multi-Limbed Yoga Systems Limbs Source Period Limbs Listed 6 Maitrī Upaniṣad last centuries BCE (debated) Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra, Dhyāna, Dhāraṇā, Tarka, Samādhi 8 Yoga Sūtras c. 325–425 CE Yama, Niyama, Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra, Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi 6 Vivekamārtaṇḍa / Gorakṣaśataka 13th–14th c. CE Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra, Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi 4 Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā c. 1450 CE Āsana, Kumbhaka (Prāṇāyāma), Mudrā, Nādānusandhāna (as its four chapters) 15 Aparōkṣānubhūti (attrib. Śaṅkara) medieval Vedāntic reinterpretation: yama, niyama, tyāga, mauna, deśa, kāla, āsana, mūlabandha, dehasāmya, dṛk-sthiti, prāṇasaṃyamana, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, ātmadhyāna, samādhi 7 Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā c. 1700 CE Ṣaṭkarma, Āsana, Mudrā, Pratyāhāra, Prāṇāyāma, Dhyāna, Samādhi

The differences are instructive. The Maitrī Upaniṣad’s six-limbed system, which reappears in the Śaiva Tantras (Chapter 5), omits yama, niyama and āsana. The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā replaces the ethical limbs with ṣaṭkarma and mudrā, reflecting the Haṭha emphasis on physical purification. The Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā’s four chapters treat āsana, prāṇāyāma, mudrā and nāda as the pillars of practice; the six-limbed Haṭha texts drop yama and niyama altogether, and the Dattātreyayogaśāstra declares that anyone who practises — brahmin, ascetic, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist — will attain success (Mallinson and Singleton 2017). The Advaita Aparōkṣānubhūti turns each limb into an aspect of the knowledge of Brahman (Chapter 4). Patañjali’s eight limbs were thus widely known and constantly reinterpreted: kept in name, they were filled with Tantric, Haṭha or Vedāntic content.

docs.title: 2.6 Pāda III: Vibhūti Pāda — The Chapter on Powers
docs.text: After defining the three internal limbs and saṃyama, the third chapter analyses the transformations of the mind and the extraordinary powers (vibhūtis or siddhis) said to arise from saṃyama.

docs.title: 2.6.1 The Three Transformations of the Mind
docs.text:
Sūtras 3.9–3.12

vyutthāna-nirodha-saṃskārayor abhibhava-prādurbhāvau nirodha-kṣaṇa-cittānvayo nirodha-pariṇāmaḥ tasya praśānta-vāhitā saṃskārāt sarvārthataikāgratayoḥ kṣayodayau cittasya samādhi-pariṇāmaḥ tataḥ punaḥ śāntoditau tulya-pratyayau cittasyaikāgratā-pariṇāmaḥ Nirodha-pariṇāma: The suppression of the rising impressions and the arising of the impressions of restraint. Samādhi-pariṇāma: The decline of all-pointedness and the rise of one-pointedness. Ekāgratā-pariṇāma: When the subsiding and arising cognitions are identical — one-pointed transformation.

The three transformations describe the deepening of practice from the side of the mind: first the impressions of restraint overcome the impressions of outward activity, so that the mind flows calmly; then many-pointedness gives way to one-pointedness; finally the cognition that fades and the cognition that arises are the same. The next sūtra (3.13) extends the analysis to all things, distinguishing change of property (dharma), of temporal character (lakṣaṇa: past, present, future) and of condition (avasthā); Vyāsa’s commentary here engages directly with Sarvāstivāda Buddhist debates on time and change.

docs.title: 2.6.2 The Siddhis
docs.text:
Patañjali describes numerous siddhis that, according to the text, arise from saṃyama on various objects (Table 2.7). These are claims of the tradition, not demonstrated abilities; scholars have noted that the chapter places Yoga within a wider Indian culture of ascetic power (White 2009).

Table 2.7. Selected Siddhis from the Vibhūti Pāda Object of Saṃyama Resultant Siddhi Sūtra Three transformations (of citta) Knowledge of past and future 3.16 Sounds of living beings Understanding of all languages 3.17 Saṃskāras (latent impressions) Knowledge of previous births 3.18 The form of one’s body Invisibility (antardhāna) 3.21 Strengths (bala) The strength of an elephant and the like 3.24 The Sun Knowledge of the worlds (bhuvana-jñāna) 3.26 The Moon Knowledge of the stars 3.27 The pole star (Dhruva) Knowledge of the movement of stars 3.28 The navel centre Knowledge of the body’s arrangement 3.29 The throat pit Cessation of hunger and thirst 3.30 Kūrma Nāḍī Steadiness (sthairya) 3.31 The light in the head Vision of perfected beings (siddhas) 3.32 Pratībha (intuitive flash) Knowledge of everything 3.33

Patañjali himself issues a caution regarding these powers:

Sūtra 3.37

te samādhāv upasargā vyutthāne siddhayaḥ These (siddhis) are obstacles to samādhi, though they are powers in the externalized state.

Whatever their status, the text treats the siddhis as obstacles (upasarga) to the goal of kaivalya; the yogin is to renounce them and continue towards liberation (cf. 3.50).

docs.title: 2.7 Pāda IV: Kaivalya Pāda — The Chapter on Liberation
docs.text: The final chapter addresses the subtlest questions of the system: the sources of the powers, the mechanism of karma, the relation between mind and object, and liberation.

docs.title: 2.7.1 Powers, Karma and Impressions
docs.text:
Powers, the chapter begins, arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (janmāuṣadhi-mantra-tapaḥ-samādhi-jāḥ siddhayaḥ, 4.1). It then analyses karma:

Sūtra 4.7–4.8

karmāśuklākṛṣṇaṃ yoginas tri-vidham itareṣām tatas tad-vipākānuguṇānām evābhivyaktir vāsanānām The karma of the yogi is neither white nor black; for others, it is threefold. From that, only those latent impressions corresponding to the fruits of karma manifest.

Every experience leaves a trace (saṃskāra) in the mind, and accumulated impressions form latent tendencies (vāsanā) that shape later perception and action. They survive even across births: there is continuity of memory and impressions “even when separated by birth, place, and time, because they are identical in form” (jāti-deśa-kāla-vyavahitānām apy ānantaryaṃ smṛti-saṃskārayor eka-rūpatvāt, 4.9). Yoga interrupts the cycle of action, impression, tendency and desire by destroying the impressions themselves (Figure 2.4). Modern readers often compare this with the psychology of habit and implicit memory; the comparison is illuminating, but Patañjali should not be read as anticipating modern psychology.

Figure 2.4. The Saṃskāra Cycle and How Yoga Breaks It: Actions create impressions, which form tendencies, which generate desires, which motivate further actions. Yoga interrupts this cycle through abhyāsa and vairāgya.

docs.title: 2.7.2 The Cloud of Dharma and Liberation
docs.text:
The last stage before liberation is called the “cloud of dharma”:

Yoga Sūtra 4.29

prasaṃkhyāne'py akusīdasya sarvathā viveka-khyāter dharma-meghaḥ samādhiḥ For one who has no interest even in the highest meditation, and who possesses constant discriminative discernment, there arises the samādhi known as “the Cloud of Dharma.”

From it, the sūtras continue, comes the cessation of the afflictions and of karma (4.30). The work ends with a definition of liberation:

Sūtra 4.34 — The Concluding Sūtra

puruṣārtha-śūnyānāṃ guṇānāṃ pratiprasavaḥ kaivalyaṃ svarūpa-pratiṣṭhā vā citi-śaktir iti Kaivalya is the counter-involution of the guṇas, which are devoid of purpose for the Puruṣa; or it is the establishment of the power of consciousness (citi-śakti) in its own nature.

When discriminative knowledge is firmly established, nature has done all it can for the Puruṣa: its constituents resolve back into their source (pratiprasava), and consciousness stands alone in its own nature. “Isolation” (kaivalya) is the Sāṃkhya-Yoga name for this freedom.

docs.title: 2.8 The Commentarial Tradition
docs.text:
The Yoga Sūtras have inspired a commentarial tradition spanning some fifteen centuries (Table 2.8), surveyed work by work in the Yoga volume of the Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies (Larson and Bhattacharya 2008). The commentaries are not only aids to reading the sūtras; they are the record of how Patañjali’s yoga was understood, argued over and adapted to the dominant philosophies of each period, and most of what is now taught as “the meaning” of a sūtra comes from one of them.

Table 2.8. Major Commentaries on the Yoga Sūtras Commentary Author Period Significance Yoga Bhāṣya Vyāsa c. 4th–5th c. Earliest; foundational; inseparable from the Sūtras Vivaraṇa attributed to Śaṅkara 8th c. or later (disputed) Sub-commentary on the Bhāṣya; authorship debated Tattvavaiśāradī Vācaspati Miśra c. 950 Sub-commentary on Vyāsa’s Bhāṣya Rājamārtaṇḍa Bhoja of Dhārā c. 1040 Royal commentary on the sūtras alone Yoga Vārttika Vijñānabhikṣu after c. 1550 Reconciles Yoga with Vedānta Maṇiprabhā Rāmānanda Sarasvatī 16th–17th c. Advaitic interpretation Yogasiddhāntacandrikā Nārāyaṇatīrtha probably 17th c. Places other yogas, including Haṭha and bhakti, within the eight limbs Bhāsvatī Hariharānanda Āraṇya 20th c. Modern Sāṃkhya-Yoga sub-commentary

docs.title: 2.8.1 One Book or Two? The Sūtras and the Bhāṣya
docs.text:
Section 2.1 noted Philipp Maas’s argument that the sūtras and the Bhāṣya were composed and transmitted as one work. The commentarial tradition is itself part of the evidence. The chapter colophons of the printed text call the whole “Patañjali’s treatise on yoga, the exposition of Sāṃkhya” (pātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre); the further words “in the commentary of the venerable Vyāsa” that follow in the printed colophons come, Maas notes, from comparatively recent paper manuscripts. Al-Bīrūnī, around 1030, took the work to be a single book of Patañjali consisting of text and explanation (Section 2.8.5). King Bhoja of Mālava, who wrote his own commentary on the sūtras alone around 1040, compares himself in a benedictory verse to the serpent-king, that is, to Patañjali in his mythical form as Śeṣa, who removed the impurities of speech, mind and body by writing on grammar, yoga and medicine — the same triple legacy that the later invocation at the head of this chapter celebrates. The attribution of the Bhāṣya to Vyāsa appears in the introductory verses of Vācaspati Miśra’s sub-commentary of about 950, although Vācaspati’s works are not consistent on the point, and the oldest unambiguous statement that sūtra and Bhāṣya had different authors that Maas could find is in Mādhava’s fourteenth-century survey of the systems, the Sarvadarśanasaṁgraha. The modern habit of speaking of “Patañjali and Vyāsa” as two authors therefore rests on a late and uncertain tradition (Maas 2013).

The question matters for interpretation. If the prose is Patañjali’s own, it is the author’s explanation of his sūtras, not the first of many possible readings, and the frequent modern practice of reading the sūtras without the Bhāṣya, or against it, loses its main justification. Many scholars still prefer to leave authorship open, but there is broad agreement that the sūtras cannot be understood apart from the Bhāṣya, and that the later commentators, from the Vivaraṇa onwards, comment on the two together.

docs.title: 2.8.2 The Vivaraṇa and the Śaṅkara Question
docs.text:
In 1952 the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library in Madras published, from South Indian manuscripts, a commentary on the sūtras and Bhāṣya called the Pātañjalayogaśāstravivaraṇa. Its chapter colophons name its author with the formal title used for Śaṅkara, the Advaita Vedāntin (c. 700–750 CE; the traditional date, 788–820, rests on later sources and long served as the conventional date in scholarship): pupil of Govinda, wandering ascetic of the highest order, Śaṅkarabhagavat. The editors accepted the attribution, and for more than half a century the Vivaraṇa has been at the centre of a debate.

Paul Hacker had noticed features of Śaṅkara’s Vedānta that suggested an early familiarity with Yoga, and in 1968 he proposed that Śaṅkara had been a follower of Yoga in his youth before he became an Advaitin, a hypothesis that presupposed rather than proved the identity of the two authors. Trevor Leggett translated the whole work as Śaṅkara’s (1990). Wilhelm Halbfass pointed to striking parallels between arguments in the Vivaraṇa and in Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, but also showed that Śaṅkara’s attitude to Sāṃkhya metaphysics and to Yoga as a path to liberation, as stated in his major works, is very hard to reconcile with the Vivaraṇa’s commitment to Patañjali. T. S. Rukmani, who also translated the work, argued that it was much later, between the eleventh and fourteenth centuries, and that it knew Vācaspati’s commentary; Kengo Harimoto and Maas have answered that the passages she cited do not show this (Maas 2013).

Whoever its author was, the Vivaraṇa matters. The latest author it clearly refers to is the Mīmāṃsā philosopher Kumārila (7th century); the text of the Bhāṣya on which it comments preserves old readings lost from most manuscripts; and it explains many difficult passages on which Vācaspati is silent. It is therefore probably the oldest surviving commentary on the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, and it records debates between Sāṃkhya-Yoga and the Buddhist and Brahmanical schools of the second half of the first millennium. Its treatment of Īśvara is notable: in commenting on YS 1.23–1.28 its author goes to great lengths to establish the existence of God by reasoning. Harimoto has edited that section critically (2014), and a full critical edition is still awaited (Harimoto 2014). The question of authorship can only be settled, as Maas puts it, by systematic comparison of style once reliable editions of both the Vivaraṇa and Śaṅkara’s works exist.

docs.title: 2.8.3 Vācaspati Miśra and King Bhoja
docs.text:
