Vācaspati Miśra of Mithilā (mid-10th century) wrote standard commentaries on almost every Brahmanical system: on Nyāya, on Sāṃkhya (the Tattvakaumudī on the Sāṃkhyakārikā), on Mīmāṃsā, and on Śaṅkara’s Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (the Bhāmatī). His Tattvavaiśāradī on the Yoga Bhāṣya expounds the text from inside the system, as a Sāṃkhya-Yoga śāstra among others, and it became the most widely copied and printed of the sub-commentaries; much of the standard modern explanation of the Yoga Sūtras, such as the systematic classification of the stages of samādhi, reaches modern readers through it. It was printed with the Bhāṣya in Calcutta in 1874 and in the Ānandāśrama edition of 1904, and James Haughton Woods’s English translation of 1914 rendered the sūtras, the Bhāṣya and Vācaspati’s commentary together (Maas 2013; Woods 1914).

Bhoja, the Paramāra king of Dhārā in Mālava (r. c. 1010–1055), a celebrated patron and the author of works on poetics, architecture and medicine, wrote the Rājamārtaṇḍa (also called the Bhojavṛtti) around 1040. Unlike Vācaspati he comments on the sūtras alone, briefly and in his own words, and in his introductory verses he criticises earlier commentators for passing over what is difficult and dwelling at length on what is plain. Its brevity made it popular: the early English translations, James Ballantyne’s (1852) and Rājendralāl Mitra’s Yoga Aphorisms of Patanjali (1883), both followed Bhoja (Maas 2013; White 2014).

docs.title: 2.8.4 Vijñānabhikṣu and the Late Commentators
docs.text:
The most ambitious later commentator was Vijñānabhikṣu, who worked in North India some time after 1550. His Yogavārttika, a long sub-commentary on the Bhāṣya, his digest the Yogasārasaṁgraha, and his works on Sāṃkhya and on the Brahmasūtra together argue that Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Vedānta, rightly understood, teach a single doctrine, in which the selves are both different from and non-different from Brahman (a form of bhedābheda that he called “non-separation”, avibhāga). He criticised Śaṅkara’s Advaita as a “crypto-Buddhist” doctrine of illusion, and he read Patañjali’s Īśvara in a strongly theistic way. Andrew Nicholson has argued that this project of reading the orthodox systems as one philosophy, of which Vijñānabhikṣu was an important early representative, prepared the ground for the modern presentation of the orthodox systems as branches of a single “Hindu philosophy” (Nicholson 2010). Vijñānabhikṣu is also, on several points, a bold interpreter rather than a faithful one: Maas shows, for example, that his reading of YS 2.27 contradicts the explanation the Bhāṣya itself gives in the next sentence (Maas 2013).

After him the commentaries multiply. Rāmānanda Sarasvatī’s Maṇiprabhā and the grammarian Nāgeśabhaṭṭa’s Vṛtti (early 18th century) are short explanations of the sūtras; Bhāvāgaṇeśa, a pupil of Vijñānabhikṣu, condensed his teacher’s views; and Nārāyaṇatīrtha, who commented on the sūtras twice, in the Yogasiddhāntacandrikā and the shorter Sūtrārthabodhinī, presented the sūtras as a framework into which the other recognised yogas, including Haṭha Yoga and the yoga of devotion, could be fitted. That last move shows how far the tradition had travelled. By the early modern period the Yoga Sūtra was being read alongside the Haṭha texts and the Bhāgavata, and Haṭha authors in turn borrowed Patañjali’s eight limbs (Chapter 7). In the nineteenth century the Bhāṣya with Vācaspati’s and Bhoja’s commentaries was printed in Calcutta, Benares and Poona, and these printed editions, rather than living teaching lineages, became the basis of the European translations and of Vivekānanda’s Rāja Yoga (1896). The last major commentary in the classical manner is the Bhāsvatī of Hariharānanda Āraṇya (1869–1947), the founder of the Kāpil Maṭh at Madhupur in Jharkhand, which continues to teach Sāṃkhya-Yoga as a monastic tradition.

docs.title: 2.8.5 The Yoga Sūtra in Arabic: al-Bīrūnī’s Kitāb Pātanjal
docs.text:
All the commentaries in Table 2.8 were written in Sanskrit. The earliest known rendering of the Yoga Sūtra into another language was made in Arabic in the early eleventh century by Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī (973–after 1050), the Central Asian scholar who came to north-western India in the train of Maḥmūd of Ghazna, learned Sanskrit from Indian pandits, and wrote the most searching account of Indian learning produced by any outsider before modern times (his work on Indian mathematics and astronomy is discussed in Volume 11, Gaṇita, and Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa). In the preface to that survey, the Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind (“Inquiry into what belongs to India”, c. 1030), he says that he had already translated two Indian books into Arabic, one on the origin and nature of created things, that is, a Sāṃkhya work, and one by Patañjali on the release of the soul from its bondage to the body. The second, the Kitāb Pātanjal, survives in a single manuscript in Istanbul, which was identified and published by Hellmut Ritter only in 1956; Shlomo Pines and Tuvia Gelblum later translated it into English, chapter by chapter, in a series of articles beginning in 1966 (Pines and Gelblum 1966).

The Kitāb Pātanjal is not a word-for-word translation. Al-Bīrūnī recast the sūtras, together with explanations drawn from a commentary, as a dialogue in which an ascetic asks questions and a sage answers them, and he rephrased Indian technical terms in the vocabulary of Arabic philosophy so that a Muslim reader could follow the argument. The explanations do not simply reproduce Vyāsa’s Bhāṣya, and which commentary he used, or whether he combined several, is still debated. His treatment of Īśvara (YS 1.23–1.29) leans towards a monotheistic reading, in line with his general view, stated in the Taḥqīq, that the learned among the Hindus believed in one God, while the polytheism he saw around him belonged to the common people. In the same work he quotes Patañjali repeatedly beside the Bhagavad Gītā and Sāṃkhya, and compares the yogic path to release with the teachings of the Sufis (White 2014).

The translation matters to the history of Yoga in two ways. First, it is the earliest witness to the text from outside the Sanskrit commentarial tradition, and it shows that in the early eleventh century Patañjali’s work was regarded in India as a leading authority on liberation — which supports the view that any eclipse of the text came later (Section 2.10). Secondly, its later influence was slight: there is little evidence that the Kitāb Pātanjal circulated widely in the Islamic world. When Muslims in India took a sustained interest in yoga in the following centuries, they met it as the practice of living Nāth and other yogis, through texts such as the Amṛtakuṇḍa, rather than through Patañjali (Chapter 7, Section 7.17).

docs.title: 2.8.6 Patañjali in Java: the Dharma Pātañjala
docs.text: A second witness from outside the Sanskrit commentaries comes from Indonesia. Among the Old Javanese and Sanskrit scriptures of the Śaiva religion of pre-Islamic Java is a text called the Dharma Pātañjala, preserved in a single fifteenth-century palm-leaf manuscript from West Java. Its first part sets out a Śaiva theology close to the Śaiva Siddhānta; its long second part is a yoga section that follows the first three chapters of the Yoga Sūtra and explains them in Old Javanese prose. Andrea Acri, who edited and translated the text, has shown that this prose often resembles the Bhāṣya but departs from it in places, and that some of its doctrinal details agree with other commentaries and with al-Bīrūnī’s Arabic version. Where most Old Javanese works teach the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) of the Śaiva scriptures, the Dharma Pātañjala keeps Patañjali’s eight limbs, recast within a Śaiva framework (Acri 2011). Like the Kitāb Pātanjal, it shows that Patañjali’s work travelled with its explanations and was read by people who understood it in their own theological terms; unlike al-Bīrūnī’s translation, it was the scripture of a living religious community.

docs.title: 2.9 Citta: Patañjali’s Theory of Mind
docs.text:
Citta is not simply “mind” in the modern sense but the whole field of mental activity through which Puruṣa (pure awareness) experiences the world. Patañjali does not himself define it in these terms. The commentators equate it with the Sāṃkhya “inner instrument” (antaḥkaraṇa), which later Vedāntic works analyse into three or four functions: manas, the sensory-motor mind that receives impressions and co-ordinates action; buddhi, the intellect that determines and discriminates; and ahaṃkāra, the “I-maker” that appropriates experience as one’s own. Vyāsa’s Bhāṣya also classifies the states of citta by the predominance of the three guṇas (Table 2.9).

Table 2.9. The Five States (Bhūmis) of Citta According to Vyāsa State Sanskrit Dominant Guṇa Characteristics Scattered Kṣipta Rajas Restless; agitated; unable to concentrate Dull Mūḍha Tamas Heavy; lethargic; prone to sleep and delusion Oscillating Vikṣipta Rajas-Sattva Occasionally focused but easily distracted One-pointed Ekāgra Sattva Concentrated; capable of sustained attention Restrained Niruddha Sattva (transcended) All vṛttis ceased; Yoga is achieved

Vyāsa adds that the first three states are not yoga. Even the oscillating mind, with its moments of focus, is unstable; yoga properly begins with the one-pointed mind and is complete in the restrained one.

docs.title: 2.9.1 Patañjali and Modern Psychology
docs.text:
The Yoga Sūtras contain a detailed psychology of attention, memory and affliction (Indian theories of mind are treated more fully in Volume 22, Manas and Śikṣā), and modern readers often set it beside clinical psychology. Patañjali’s analysis of the kleśas, for example, is read today as an account of the roots of psychological suffering, with ignorance as cognitive distortion, egoism as a rigid self-image and clinging to life as existential anxiety. Such comparisons are heuristic. Unlike modern clinical psychology, which is oriented to health and adaptation, Patañjali’s system begins from a soteriological goal and analyses the mind in terms of what obstructs it (Table 2.10).

Table 2.10. Comparative Framework: Patañjali and Modern Psychology Aspect Patañjali’s System Modern Western Psychology Goal Liberation of consciousness (kaivalya) Adaptation, well-being, symptom reduction Model of mind Citta as instrument of Puruṣa; mind is not the self Mind as emergent property of brain; self is mental construct Unconscious Saṃskāras and vāsanās: latent impressions accumulated across lifetimes Unconscious drives (Freud); implicit memory (cognitive science) Suffering Kleśas: five root afflictions rooted in ignorance Psychological disorders rooted in maladaptive patterns Method Systematic sādhana: ethical conduct, posture, breath, meditation Talk therapy, pharmacology, behavioural modification Evidence First-person experiential verification through samādhi Third-person empirical measurement

docs.title: 2.10 The Fortunes of the Yoga Sūtra
docs.text:
How much the Yoga Sūtra mattered in India between the commentators and the moderns is debated. David Gordon White has argued that the text was little read between roughly the twelfth and the nineteenth centuries, and that it owes its present status as “the” scripture of Yoga largely to colonial-era Indologists, to Vivekānanda’s Rāja Yoga (1896) and to later modern teachers (White 2014). The second half of the thesis is widely accepted: the nineteenth-century printed editions and translations, not living teaching lineages, made the sūtras the canonical text of modern yoga. The first half is contested. The commentaries of Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nārāyaṇatīrtha and Nāgeśa (Section 2.8.4) show that the sūtras continued to be studied and argued over by Sanskrit scholars in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries; Haṭha and Vedānta authors borrowed their eight limbs; and Advaitins such as Vidyāraṇya quoted them as an authority on stilling the mind (Chapter 4). What seems to have declined in the second millennium is not scholarly attention but the text’s place as a guide to practice, which passed largely to the Haṭha and Tantric manuals (Maas 2013; Larson and Bhattacharya 2008).

The sūtras’ central claims — about samādhi, the separateness of puruṣa and the attainment of kaivalya — are metaphysical and experiential claims that lie beyond the reach of empirical investigation; the tradition grounds them in the testimony of accomplished practitioners. Their analysis of attention and of the afflictions invites comparison with modern research on attention and mindfulness, but such comparisons are analogies rather than confirmations.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Karma Yoga and Bhakti Yoga
docs.text:
Bhagavad Gītā 3.19

tasmād asaktaḥ satataṃ kāryaṃ karma samācara asakto hy ācaran karma param āpnoti pūruṣaḥ Therefore, always perform action that must be done, without attachment. For by performing action without attachment, one attains the Supreme.

Part A: Karma Yoga — The Path of Selfless Action

docs.title: 3.1 The Meaning of Karma Yoga
docs.text:
Karma Yoga is the discipline of acting without attachment to results (phala): one performs one’s duties (svadharma) and offers the action to God, so that ordinary activity becomes a means of liberation rather than a cause of bondage. The word karma, from the root kṛ (“to do”), means action and, by extension, ritual action and the consequences of action. The idea answered a problem that the renunciant traditions had made acute. If action binds the self to rebirth, as Buddhists, Jains and the Upaniṣadic renouncers taught, must the seeker of liberation abandon the world? The Gītā’s answer is that bondage comes not from action but from desire for its fruits.

Definition: Karma Yoga

Karma Yoga is the discipline of performing all actions as an offering to the Divine, without attachment to their fruits, maintaining equanimity in success and failure, and thereby purifying the mind and attaining liberation through action itself.

docs.title: 3.2 The Bhagavad Gītā and Karma Yoga
docs.text: The Bhagavad Gītā, part of the Bhīṣma Parva of the Mahābhārata and probably composed between the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE (Malinar 2007), is the foremost scripture of Karma Yoga. Kṛṣṇa’s teaching to Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra is the classic exposition of selfless action in Indian thought, and every major school of Vedānta commented on it; Śaṅkara’s commentary, the oldest to survive, is available in Gambhirananda’s translation (Śaṅkarācārya 1997).

docs.title: 3.2.1 The Dilemma of Arjuna
docs.text:
The Gītā opens with Arjuna’s crisis: faced with the prospect of fighting against his own kinsmen, teachers, and elders, the great warrior is overwhelmed with grief and confusion. He throws down his bow and declares that he will not fight. It is in response to this existential crisis that Kṛṣṇa unfolds the teaching of Karma Yoga (Figure 3.1).

Figure 3.1. Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna in the chariot, with Hanumān on the banner (Indian miniature painting, British Museum). Painting: unknown artist, British Museum; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.2.2 Key Teachings on Karma Yoga
docs.text:
Gītā 2.47 — The Cardinal Verse of Karma Yoga

karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadā cana mā karma-phala-hetur bhūr mā te saṅgo'stv akarmaṇi Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.

This is perhaps the most quoted verse of the Gītā. It is built of negations: the agent has no claim to the fruits, must not let them be his motive, and must not, for all that, fall back on inaction. The next verse defines yoga itself in these terms, as equanimity:

Gītā 2.48 — Yoga as Equanimity

yoga-sthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanaṃjaya siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate Established in Yoga, perform actions, O Dhanañjaya, abandoning attachment, remaining equal in success and failure. This equanimity is called Yoga.

Gītā 3.9 — Action as Sacrifice

yajñārthāt karmaṇo'nyatra loko'yaṃ karma-bandhanaḥ tad-arthaṃ karma kaunteya mukta-saṅgaḥ samācara The world is bound by actions other than those performed as sacrifice. Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.

docs.title: 3.2.3 Niṣkāma Karma: Desireless Action
docs.text: The later tradition summed up this teaching as niṣkāma karma, action without desire for personal gain, and contrasted it with sakāma karma, action driven by desire. The first is done as duty, service or an offering to God; its agent regards himself as an instrument rather than the doer and stays equal in success and failure; and it leads to liberation. The second is done for reward, binds its agent to the outcome, breeds anxiety and leads to further rebirth. The Gītā’s own image for desireless action is sacrifice: action done as an offering does not bind.

docs.title: 3.2.4 Lokasaṃgraha: Action for the Welfare of the World
docs.text:
Kṛṣṇa introduces another powerful motivation for action: lokasaṃgraha — action performed for the welfare and cohesion of the world:

Gītā 3.20–3.21

karmaṇaiva hi saṃsiddhim āsthitā janakādayaḥ loka-saṃgraham evāpi saṃpaśyan kartum arhasi yad yad ācarati śreṣṭhas tat tad evetaro janaḥ sa yat pramāṇaṃ kurute lokas tad anuvartate By action alone, Janaka and others attained perfection. You should act with a view to the welfare of the world. Whatever a great person does, common people follow. Whatever standard he sets, the world follows.

docs.title: 3.3 The Philosophy of Action and Non-Action
docs.text:
The Gītā contains a subtle and profound analysis of the nature of action:

Gītā 4.18

karmaṇy akarma yaḥ paśyed akarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ sa buddhimān manuṣyeṣu sa yuktaḥ kṛtsna-karma-kṛt One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction — that person is wise among human beings, a yogi, a doer of all actions.

The commentators read this verse in the light of the Gītā’s Sāṃkhya: the self is never an agent (akartā), all action belongs to nature (prakṛti) and its constituents, and the wise person acts in the world while knowing that he does not act. For Śaṅkara the verse shows why action can never itself be the means of liberation (Chapter 4); for theistic commentators it shows how action offered to God ceases to bind.

Gītā 5.8–5.9

naiva kiṃ cit karomīti yukto manyeta tattva-vit paśyañ śṛṇvan spṛśañ jighrann aśnan gacchan svapañ śvasan pralapan visṛjan gṛhṇann unmiṣan nimiṣann api indriyāṇīndriyārtheṣu vartanta iti dhārayan The one who knows the truth thinks “I do nothing at all” — while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing, speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and closing the eyes — knowing that it is only the senses interacting with their objects.

docs.title: 3.4 Karma, Duty and the Gītā’s Social Setting
docs.text: Karma Yoga presupposes the doctrine of karma, which is treated with the darśanas in Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa. Later Vedāntic texts divide karma into three stores: the karma accumulated in past lives (sañcita); the portion of it that has begun to bear fruit in the present body (prārabdha); and the karma now being made, which will bear fruit in future (āgāmin, also called kriyamāṇa, “what is being done”). Advaita texts such as the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi teach that knowledge burns the first and the third, while the second must be exhausted by experience even by the liberated person (Chapter 4). In these terms the Karma Yogin’s desireless action adds nothing to the future store, and his equanimity lets the fructifying karma run out without new entanglement. The Gītā itself analyses every action into five factors — the body as its seat, the agent, the various instruments, the various efforts and, fifth, the unseen or divine (daiva) (18.14) — so that the self, which is none of these, is not the doer.

docs.title: 3.4.1 Svadharma: One’s Own Duty
docs.text:
Central to the Gītā’s teaching on action is svadharma, the duty that falls to a person by nature (svabhāva) and station:

Gītā 3.35

śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt sv-anuṣṭhitāt sva-dharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ para-dharmo bhayāvahaḥ Better is one’s own dharma, though imperfectly performed, than the dharma of another well performed. Death in one’s own dharma is better; the dharma of another is fraught with danger.

In the Gītā’s own context, svadharma is the duty of one’s varṇa: Arjuna must fight because he is a kṣatriya, and the text states that the four varṇas were created by Kṛṣṇa according to quality and action (4.13) and lists the duties proper to each (18.41–48). This aspect of the text has been read in sharply different ways. B.R. Ambedkar saw the Gītā as a defence of the caste order and of brahmanical orthodoxy (Ambedkar 1987). Modern Hindu interpreters such as Tilak, Aurobindo and Gandhi instead read svadharma as one’s individual nature and vocation (Section 3.13), and many devotional traditions stressed the verse that opens the highest goal to women, vaiśyas and śūdras who take refuge in Kṛṣṇa (9.32). The same verse contains the compound pāpayonayaḥ, “of sinful birth”. On one construal, which many translators follow, it describes the women, vaiśyas and śūdras; on another, it names a further group, “even those of sinful birth”, alongside them (Malinar 2007). Either way, the verse opens the path while reflecting the hierarchy it addressed, and a reader should recognise both the social setting of the teaching and the universalising readings it has inspired. Read in the second way, the Karma Yogin is called to perform the duties that fall to him or her — as parent, teacher, farmer, artist or official — with skill and without selfish motive.

Part B: Bhakti Yoga — The Path of Divine Love

docs.title: 3.5 The Meaning of Bhakti
docs.text:
Bhakti is derived from the Sanskrit root bhaj, “to share in”, “to partake”, and hence “to serve, worship, love”. Bhakti Yoga is the discipline of devotion to a personal God, cultivated until it becomes complete surrender. In the Gītā it is one of the forms that yoga takes; in the later devotional traditions the relation was often reversed, and yoga became one of the forms, or one of the rivals, of devotion.

Nārada Bhakti Sūtra 2

sā tv asmin para-prema-rūpā That (Bhakti) is of the nature of supreme love for God.

Nārada Bhakti Sūtra 3–4

amṛta-svarūpā ca yal labdhvā pumān siddho bhavaty amṛto bhavati tṛpto bhavati It is of the nature of immortal bliss. Having obtained it, a person becomes perfected, immortal, and completely satisfied.

docs.title: 3.6 Bhakti in the Bhagavad Gītā
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā, particularly Chapters 9 and 12, contains some of the most moving teachings on Bhakti Yoga:

Gītā 9.26

patraṃ puṣpaṃ phalaṃ toyaṃ yo me bhaktyā prayacchati tad ahaṃ bhakty-upahṛtam aśnāmi prayatātmanaḥ Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water — that offering of devotion from the pure-hearted I accept.

Gītā 9.34

man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṃ namaskuru mām evaiṣyasi yuktvaivam ātmānaṃ mat-parāyaṇaḥ Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, bow to Me. Absorbed in Me, with Me as your supreme goal, you shall come to Me.

Gītā 18.65–18.66 — The Supreme Secret

man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṃ namaskuru mām evaiṣyasi satyaṃ te pratijāne priyo'si me sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja ahaṃ tvāṃ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, bow to Me. Truly I promise you: you are dear to Me. Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone. I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve.

docs.title: 3.7 The Navadhā Bhakti: Nine Forms of Devotion
docs.text:
The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (c. 9th–10th century CE) presents the celebrated nine-fold path of devotion (navadhā bhakti), spoken by the child-devotee Prahlāda to his father Hiraṇyakaśipu (Table 3.1):

Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5.23

śravaṇaṃ kīrtanaṃ viṣṇoḥ smaraṇaṃ pāda-sevanam arcanaṃ vandanaṃ dāsyaṃ sakhyam ātma-nivedanam Hearing, chanting, remembering, serving the feet, worshipping, saluting, servitude, friendship, and complete self-surrender — these are the nine forms of Bhakti to Lord Viṣṇu.

Table 3.1. The Nine Forms of Bhakti (Navadhā Bhakti), with the exemplars named in later tradition No. Form English Description Exemplar 1 Śravaṇa Hearing Listening to the Lord’s name, glories, and deeds Parīkṣit 2 Kīrtana Chanting Singing the praises and names of the Lord Śuka 3 Smaraṇa Remembering Constant remembrance of the Lord Prahlāda 4 Pāda-sevana Serving the feet Humble service to the Lord’s lotus feet Lakṣmī 5 Arcana Worship Ritual worship with offerings Pṛthu 6 Vandana Salutation Prostration and prayer Akrūra 7 Dāsya Servitude Regarding oneself as the Lord’s servant Hanumān 8 Sakhya Friendship Relating to the Lord as an intimate friend Arjuna 9 Ātma-nivedana Self-surrender Complete offering of oneself to the Lord Bali

docs.title: 3.8 The Nārada Bhakti Sūtra
docs.text: The Nārada Bhakti Sūtra is a celebrated treatise on the philosophy and practice of Bhakti, attributed to the celestial sage Nārada. It consists of 84 aphorisms that define, describe, and extol the path of divine love (Nārada 1943). Its date is uncertain; it draws on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and is generally regarded as a medieval work.

docs.title: 3.8.1 Characteristics of Supreme Bhakti
docs.text:
Nārada Bhakti Sūtra 6–7

yaj jñātvā matto bhavati stabdho bhavaty ātmārāmo bhavati sā na kāmay­amānā nirodha-rūpat­vāt Having known which, one becomes intoxicated, stunned, and delights in the Self. It (Bhakti) is not of the nature of desire, being of the nature of cessation (of all desires).

docs.title: 3.8.2 Parā and Aparā Bhakti
docs.text: The devotional treatises distinguish a lower, preparatory devotion (aparā or gauṇī bhakti) from the supreme devotion (parā bhakti) of the Nārada Sūtra’s definition. The first is mixed with desire and expressed through ritual, vows and pilgrimage; it seeks boons and protection and fluctuates with circumstance. The second is love for its own sake, steady and spontaneous; the tradition’s examples are the cowherd women (gopīs) of Vṛndāvana and, among the saints, Mīrābāī.

docs.title: 3.9 The Philosophy of Divine Love in Bhakti Yoga
3.9.1 Rasa Theory and Bhakti
docs.text:
The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition, following Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu, developed an elaborate classification of devotional emotions (rasas) that the devotee can experience in relation to the Divine (Table 3.2).

Table 3.2. The Five Primary Rasas (Devotional Relationships) in Bhakti Rasa Relationship Exemplar Character Śānta Peaceful contemplation Sanatkumāras Tranquil awareness of God’s presence Dāsya Servitude Hanumān Devoted, selfless service to the Lord Sakhya Friendship Arjuna; Sudāmā Intimate, playful companionship Vātsalya Parental love Yaśodā; Nanda Protective, nurturing affection Mādhurya Conjugal love Rādhā; Gopīs Intense, all-consuming divine love

Each rasa represents a distinct mode of relating to the Divine, and the tradition holds that the devotee is naturally drawn to the rasa that corresponds to their innermost spiritual temperament. The mādhurya rasa (the mood of conjugal love) is considered the highest, as exemplified by the Gopīs of Vṛndāvana, whose love for Kṛṣṇa was so intense that it transcended all worldly attachments.

docs.title: 3.9.2 The Concept of Prapatti (Śaraṇāgati): Total Surrender
docs.text:
The highest expression of Bhakti is prapatti or śaraṇāgati — total, unconditional surrender to the Divine. The Śrī Vaiṣṇava tradition, drawing on the Pāñcarātra Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā and Lakṣmī Tantra and as systematised by Vedānta Deśika (14th century), describes six components of śaraṇāgati (Table 3.3).

Table 3.3. The Six Components of Śaraṇāgati (Prapatti) Component Sanskrit Description Resolve to please Ānukūlya Saṃkalpa Determination to do what is pleasing to the Lord Avoidance of displeasure Prātikūlya Varjanam Avoidance of what is displeasing to the Lord Faith in protection Mahāviśvāsa Firm faith that the Lord will protect Prayer for protection Goptṛtva Varaṇam Active supplication for the Lord’s protection Surrender of self Ātma-nikṣepa Placing oneself entirely in the Lord’s hands Humility Kārpaṇya Awareness of one’s own helplessness

Stotraratna of Yāmuna (Āḷavantār), 22

na dharma-niṣṭho'smi na cātma-vedī na bhaktimāṃs tvac-caraṇāravinde ak­iñcano'nanya-gatiḥ śaraṇya tvat-pāda-mūlaṃ śaraṇaṃ prapadye I am not established in dharma, nor do I know the Self. I have no devotion to Your lotus feet. Helpless and with no other refuge, O Lord, I surrender at Your feet.

docs.title: 3.10 Devotion and Yoga in the Bhakti Movements
docs.text:
From the sixth century onwards devotional poetry in the regional languages transformed Indian religion: the Tamil Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉārs (6th–9th centuries), the Vīraśaiva vacana poets of twelfth-century Karnataka, the Vārkārīs of Maharashtra from Jñāneśvar and Nāmdev to Tukārām, the Sants of North India such as Kabīr and Ravidās, the Kṛṣṇa devotion of Sūrdās, Mīrābāī and Caitanya, and Śaṅkaradeva in Assam. Their literature is treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā; what matters here is how they related to yoga.

Three attitudes can be distinguished. The first subordinated yoga to devotion. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa keeps the eight limbs but turns meditation into loving remembrance, and in its eleventh book Kṛṣṇa calls the yogic powers distractions (Chapter 1, Section 1.5.3); the Gauḍīya theologians went further and held that the pure devotee does not even desire liberation. The second absorbed yoga into devotion. Jñāneśvar (13th century), who traced his lineage to the Nāth gurus, wrote a famous account of kuṇḍalinī in Marathi inside his commentary on the Gītā (Chapter 7, Section 7.16), and the Sants of North India, like the Sikh Gurus, used the vocabulary of Nāth yoga — the unstruck sound, the tenth door, the state of natural ease (sahaj) — for the fruits of devotion to the divine name. The third treated the yogi as a rival. Kabīr mocks the yogi’s earrings, ashes and matted hair as outward show. Patton Burchett has argued that the rise of Rāmānandī and Kṛṣṇa devotion in early modern North India was shaped by its competition with Tantric and Nāth yoga: devotional authors from Nābhādās, whose Bhaktamāl (c. 1600) is the great hagiography of the movement, onwards presented bhakti as respectable, open to all and morally superior to the power-seeking yogi and the Tantric worshipper (Burchett 2019). In the Tamil country, by contrast, the Śaiva devotional canon itself came to include a great yoga text, Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram (Chapter 5, Section 5.8).

docs.title: 3.11 Bhakti and Society
docs.text:
Bhakti as a Universal Path — and Its Limits

Bhakti teachers repeatedly declared that devotion is open to all, regardless of caste, gender or learning. The Gītā (9.32) already promises the highest goal to women, vaiśyas and śūdras who take refuge in Kṛṣṇa (on a common reading, while still calling them “of sinful birth”; Section 3.4), and the vernacular saint-poets — among them women such as Āṇṭāḷ, Akka Mahādevi and Mīrābāī, and low-caste or untouchable saints such as Cokhāmeḷā and Ravidās — composed in the languages of ordinary people rather than Sanskrit.

Historians caution, however, against treating Bhakti as a straightforward social revolution. The equality proclaimed in devotion often coexisted with caste practice in daily life: Cokhāmeḷā was revered as a saint yet barred from the Paṇḍharpur temple, and his poems lament this exclusion. Some movements, notably the Vīraśaivas of 12th-century Karnāṭaka, did attack caste directly; others reinforced brahmanical norms. The radical voices of Bhakti are best read as a sustained protest within the caste order rather than as its abolition (Hawley 2015).

docs.title: 3.12 The Integration of Karma and Bhakti
docs.text:
Karma Yoga and Bhakti Yoga are complementary rather than separate disciplines. The Gītā teaches that the highest form of Karma Yoga is Bhakti — action performed as an offering to God, motivated not by duty alone but by love:

Gītā 9.27

yat karoṣi yad aśnāsi yaj juhoṣi dadāsi yat yat tapasyasi kaunteya tat kuruṣva mad-arpaṇam Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī — do that as an offering to Me.

Action offered in love loses its power to bind, and devotion expressed as service becomes action. The theistic commentators, above all Rāmānuja, read the Gītā as teaching that both culminate in a devotion that is itself a form of knowledge, a steady and loving remembrance of God (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 3.13 Modern Readings of Karma Yoga
docs.text: In the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries Karma Yoga became the most politically consequential of the yogas. Vivekānanda’s Karma Yoga (1896) made selfless work, and service of the poor as service of God, the spiritual practice of the householder; the Ramakrishna Mission’s relief work was its institutional form. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, writing in Mandalay jail, argued in his Gītā Rahasya (1915) that the Gītā teaches energetic action in the world, not renunciation, and he rejected the Advaita reading that subordinated action to knowledge. Aurobindo’s Essays on the Gita, serialised between 1916 and 1920, read it as a synthesis of works, knowledge and devotion, the germ of his own integral yoga (Chapter 11, Section 11.4.3). Gandhi, who called his Gujarati rendering of the Gītā Anāsaktiyoga, “the yoga of non-attachment”, made desireless action the basis of a politics of non-violence and read the battle of Kurukṣetra as an allegory of the inner struggle. These readings were contested in their turn: Ambedkar’s criticism of the Gītā’s defence of varṇa (Section 3.4) was aimed partly at them. They show that the Gītā’s yoga of action, like Patañjali’s yoga of stillness, has been reinterpreted in every age.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Jñāna Yoga: Advaita Vedānta and Yoga
docs.text:
Bhagavad Gītā 3.3

loke'smin dvividhā niṣṭhā purā proktā mayānagha jñānayogena sāṃkhyānāṃ karmayogena yoginām In this world, O blameless one, a twofold path was taught by me of old: the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, the yoga of action for the yogins.

docs.title: 4.1 A Name and Its History
docs.text:
“Jñāna Yoga”, the yoga of knowledge, is an old phrase with a modern career. The Gītā uses it in the verse above for the path of the Sāṃkhyas, those who seek liberation through discriminating knowledge, and sets it beside the yoga of action. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa names three yogas, of knowledge, action and devotion (11.20). But the idea that “Jñāna Yoga” is one of four parallel paths, alongside Rāja, Karma and Bhakti Yoga, is largely Vivekānanda’s: his lectures published as Jñāna Yoga (1899) presented Advaita Vedānta under that name, and modern teaching has followed him (Chapter 1, Section 1.9).

For the classical Advaitins themselves, knowledge was not one yoga among others. It was the only direct means of liberation, and their relation to yoga — to Patañjali’s system, to meditative technique, to the Haṭha practices of their own renunciant order — was complex: they rejected yoga as a philosophy, used it as a discipline, and argued about how far it could help. That relation is the subject of this chapter. The doctrines of Advaita (the unreality of difference, superimposition, the levels of reality, the theory of māyā) are treated in Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa, and are recalled here only as far as the argument requires.

docs.title: 4.2 Knowledge Alone: The Advaita Position
docs.text:
Advaita Vedānta’s classical exponent is Śaṅkara (c. 700–750 CE; the traditional date, 788–820, rests on later sources and long served as the conventional date in scholarship). His authentic works include commentaries on the principal Upaniṣads, the Brahmasūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā, and the independent Upadeśasāhasrī; hundreds of other works, including the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi and the Ātmabodha, are attributed to him by tradition, but most scholars doubt that he wrote them (Mayeda 1979). His central claim is that the self (ātman) is identical with the absolute (brahman), and that bondage is nothing but ignorance of this identity. It follows that liberation cannot be produced by any action, ritual or meditative, since whatever is produced by action is impermanent. It can only be revealed by knowledge, which removes the ignorance as light removes the appearance of a snake in a rope.

The means to that knowledge is the study of scripture under a teacher. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad’s injunction that the self “is to be seen, heard, reflected upon and meditated upon” (ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyo maitreyi, 2.4.5) gave the Advaitins their triad of hearing (śravaṇa) the great sayings of the Upaniṣads, such as tat tvam asi (“That thou art”, in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad), reflecting on them (manana) to remove doubt, and contemplating them (nididhyāsana) until the knowledge is firm. At the opening of his Brahmasūtra commentary Śaṅkara lists the qualifications of the student: discrimination between the eternal and the transient, dispassion, a group of six virtues beginning with calm and self-control, and the desire for liberation. Advaita was above all a tradition of renunciants, and it was socially restricted: following the Dharmaśāstra, Śaṅkara held that only twice-born men were entitled to study the Veda, and in his Brahmasūtra commentary (1.3.34–38) he denied śūdras access to Vedic knowledge, although he allowed that they might attain liberation through the epics and Purāṇas. Modern Advaita teachers have generally abandoned these restrictions.

docs.title: 4.3 Śaṅkara and Yoga
docs.text:
Śaṅkara’s attitude to yoga has two sides. As a philosophy, Patañjala Yoga was for him a rival. The Brahmasūtra itself, after refuting Sāṃkhya, adds that “by this, Yoga is refuted” (etena yogaḥ pratyuktaḥ, 2.1.3). Śaṅkara explains that the yoga tradition is rejected in so far as it teaches, with Sāṃkhya, an independent primal matter as the cause of the world and a plurality of selves liberated by discriminating them from matter. Liberation does not come, he insists, from knowing the self as separate from nature, but from knowing it as Brahman.

As a discipline, however, yoga was indispensable to him. His commentary on the sixth chapter of the Gītā, which teaches the yoga of meditation (dhyānayoga), treats posture, the steadying of the mind and the withdrawal of the senses as an aid to knowledge, the means by which the mind of the renunciant is made fit to receive it. In the Brahmasūtra commentary he accepts those parts of the yoga tradition that do not contradict the Veda, and he does not doubt that the yogin’s concentration can be real. What he denies is that any such state, however exalted, is liberation in itself. This placed him in a long dispute with other Vedāntins. Maṇḍana Miśra and others held that knowledge of Brahman must be made effective by repeated meditation (prasaṅkhyāna); Śaṅkara, in the Upadeśasāhasrī, rejects the idea that meditation produces a liberation that knowledge has not already given (Mayeda 1979).

Whether Śaṅkara also wrote a commentary on the Yoga Sūtra itself, the Vivaraṇa, is still debated (Chapter 2, Section 2.8.2). Paul Hacker’s suggestion that Śaṅkara had been a follower of Yoga before he became an Advaitin would explain both the commentary and the yogic flavour of some of his early works; it would also explain why the later Advaita order took yoga so readily into its practice.

docs.title: 4.4 Before and Around Śaṅkara: Gauḍapāda’s “Yoga of No Contact”
docs.text: The oldest surviving Advaita work, the verses on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad ascribed to Gauḍapāda (Māṇḍūkyakārikā, probably 6th–7th century), already has a yoga of its own. In its third book it calls the realisation of non-duality the “yoga of no contact” (asparśayoga, 3.39), a yoga that, it says, the yogins themselves find hard to see and fear, since they mistake its fearlessness for annihilation. The same book describes the discipline of the mind with a famous image: the mind is to be restrained tirelessly, like a man emptying the ocean drop by drop with the tip of a blade of grass (3.41). The mind must be roused when it sinks into torpor and calmed when it is distracted; and the yogin must not linger in the pleasure of absorption but pass beyond it (3.44–45). These verses, which echo Buddhist meditation manuals as well as Patañjali, became the model for the Advaita treatment of meditation: technique is needed to steady the mind, but its goal is a knowledge that no technique produces.

docs.title: 4.5 The Yogavāsiṣṭha
docs.text:
The most important text for the relation between Advaita and yoga is not a work of Śaṅkara’s school at all. The Yogavāsiṣṭha or Mahārāmāyaṇa, a dialogue in which the sage Vasiṣṭha instructs the young Rāma, despairing of the world, in the way to liberation, is a vast poem in six books (prakaraṇas) and some thirty thousand verses. Walter Slaje has shown that it grew out of an earlier Kashmiri work, the Mokṣopāya (“Means to Liberation”), composed around the tenth century, which was later reworked and given a Vedāntic colouring (Slaje 1994). An abridgement, the Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha, circulated widely, and it was this version that Niẓām al-Dīn Pānīpatī put into Persian for Prince Salīm in 1597 (Chapter 7, Table 7.12).

The work’s philosophy is a thoroughgoing idealism: the world is a projection of the mind, as real and as unreal as a dream, and bondage is the mind’s attachment to its own creations. Liberation is the stilling of the mind, and the mind is stilled by two means, which Vasiṣṭha names in the book on calming (Upaśama-prakaraṇa): yoga, the restraint of the mind’s movements, and knowledge, right seeing. Because mind and breath move together, the restraint of the breath is a means to the stilling of the mind. In one of the work’s best-known stories, the ancient crow Bhusuṇḍa explains that he has outlived the dissolutions of many worlds by fixing his attention on the movement of the breath. The text also gives the fullest pre-modern portrait of the person liberated in life (jīvanmukta), who acts in the world while inwardly free, and of the latent tendencies (vāsanā) whose exhaustion makes that freedom possible (Venkatesananda 1993). Its stories, more than its metaphysics, made it one of the most widely read books of later Hindu India, and through Vidyāraṇya it became an authority for Advaitins.

docs.title: 4.6 Vidyāraṇya’s Jīvanmuktiviveka
docs.text:
The work that built Patañjali’s yoga most explicitly into Advaita practice is the Jīvanmuktiviveka (“Discrimination of Liberation in Life”) of Vidyāraṇya, the fourteenth-century head of the Śṛṅgerī monastery to whom the Pañcadaśī is also attributed (his identity with the scholar Mādhava, minister at Vijayanagara, is traditional but debated). The book is written for the renunciant who already has knowledge but is not yet free of the old habits of the mind. Liberation in life, Vidyāraṇya argues, requires three things practised together: knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), the destruction of latent tendencies (vāsanākṣaya) and the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa). Knowledge alone liberates in principle, but without the other two its fruit, the bliss and stability of the liberated person, is not secured.

For the dissolution of the mind Vidyāraṇya turns to Patañjali. He quotes the Yoga Sūtra’s definition of yoga as the cessation of the mind’s fluctuations, its account of practice and dispassion and its distinction between cognitive and non-cognitive absorption, and he quotes the Yogavāsiṣṭha at length on the stilling of the mind and the breath. He also distinguishes two kinds of renunciation: the renunciation of one who seeks knowledge (vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa) and the renunciation of one who already knows (vidvat-saṃnyāsa), whose discipline is precisely the practice of yoga for the sake of liberation in life. Andrew Fort, who has traced the history of the idea of liberation in life from Śaṅkara to the moderns, shows how far this goes beyond Śaṅkara: what for him was a by-product of knowledge became for Vidyāraṇya a state to be cultivated by yogic means (Fort 1998). The Pañcadaśī, a verse summary of Advaita in fifteen chapters, likewise devotes a chapter to the “bliss of yoga” (yogānanda).

docs.title: 4.7 Yoga in Later Advaita
docs.text:
After Vidyāraṇya, Advaita and yoga were closely interwoven. Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra (15th century), the most widely used introduction to Advaita, describes a non-dual absorption (nirvikalpa samādhi) whose auxiliaries are Patañjali’s eight limbs, and names four obstacles to it: falling into torpor (laya), distraction (vikṣepa), latent passion (kaṣāya) and enjoyment of the bliss of absorption (rasāsvāda) — the last an echo of Gauḍapāda’s warning. The Aparōkṣānubhūti, attributed to Śaṅkara but certainly later, teaches a fifteen-limbed yoga in which each limb is reinterpreted as an aspect of the knowledge of Brahman (Chapter 2, Table 2.6), and it recommends combining this yoga with Haṭha Yoga for those whose minds are not yet fully ripe. The Śivasaṃhitā frames Haṭha practice with an Advaita metaphysics, and the Yoga Upaniṣads, collected and commented on in the eighteenth century by the Advaita renunciant Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, present Haṭha Yoga as Vedāntic revelation (Chapter 7). In the same centuries the Daśanāmī renunciants of Śaṅkara’s order were among the principal practitioners of Haṭha Yoga.

Not every Vedāntin accepted this synthesis. Vijñānabhikṣu, the sixteenth-century commentator on the Yoga Sūtra, attacked Śaṅkara’s Advaita as a “crypto-Buddhist” doctrine of illusion and offered his own reconciliation of Sāṃkhya, Yoga and a theistic Vedānta (Chapter 2, Section 2.8.4). The theistic Vedāntins understood knowledge itself in yogic terms. Rāmānuja (traditionally 1017–1137) argues in his Śrībhāṣya that the “knowledge” that the Upaniṣads prescribe as the means to liberation is meditation (dhyāna, upāsana), a steady remembrance (dhruvā smṛti) of the Lord that ripens into devotion; and he, like the other theistic schools, rejected the Advaita ideal of liberation in life. Their positions are treated in Volume 3.

docs.title: 4.8 The Liberated Person
docs.text:
All these discussions turn on the figure of the person liberated in life (jīvanmukta), whom the Gītā had already described as the person of steady wisdom:

Bhagavad Gītā 2.55

prajāhāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha mano-gatān ātmany evātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthita-prajñas tadocyate When a person completely abandons all desires of the mind, O Pārtha, and is satisfied in the Self by the Self alone — then that person is called sthita-prajña (one of steady wisdom).

For Śaṅkara the body of the liberated person continues only through the momentum of the karma that had already begun to bear fruit (prārabdha), as a potter’s wheel, in the image already used by the Sāṃkhyakārikā (67), goes on turning after the potter has stopped. For Vidyāraṇya and the Yogavāsiṣṭha liberation in life is a condition with its own marks and its own discipline, protected by yoga. The difference matters for the history of yoga, because the second view gave yogic practice a permanent place in the life of the Advaita renunciant.

docs.title: 4.9 Modern Advaita and Yoga
docs.text: In the modern period the two strands separated again. Vivekānanda presented Rāja Yoga and Jñāna Yoga as distinct paths, the first a science of concentration open to people of any belief, the second the Advaita teaching of the self (Chapter 11). Bhagavān Rāmaṇa Maharṣi (1879–1950) of Tiruvaṇṇāmalai, the most widely revered Advaita teacher of the twentieth century, taught a direct “enquiry into the self” (ātma-vicāra): the practitioner traces the thought “I” (aham-vṛtti) back to its source, and finds that the individual ego has no independent reality. His short Tamil work Nāṉ Yār? (“Who am I?”) allows breath-control as an aid that quietens the mind, but only for as long as it is practised; enquiry, he held, ends the mind’s restlessness at its root. Like Gauḍapāda and Śaṅkara, Rāmaṇa valued yogic technique as preparation and denied that it was the goal. The long Advaita conversation with yoga, from the “yoga of no contact” to the enquiry “Who am I?”, is thus a conversation about the limits of technique (Fort 1998).

docs.title: Chapter 5: Tantra and Yoga
docs.text:
A traditional definition of “Tantra” (attributed to the Kāmika Āgama)

tanoti vipulān arthān tattva-mantra-samanvitān trāṇaṃ ca kurute yasmāt tantram ity abhidhīyate That which expands vast knowledge pertaining to tattva (reality) and mantra (sacred formula), and which provides protection (trāṇa) — that is called Tantra.

docs.title: 5.1 What is Tantra?
docs.text:
Tantra is one of the most misunderstood yet important traditions of Indian religion. The word tantra comes from the root tan (to stretch, to weave) with the instrumental suffix -tra; its basic meaning is “loom” or “warp”, and hence a systematic treatise. In religious usage it denotes a body of scriptures, revealed (according to their adherents) by Śiva, the Goddess, Viṣṇu or the Buddha, and the traditions of ritual and yoga based upon them. Tantric traditions are Hindu (Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava), Buddhist (Vajrayāna) and to a lesser extent Jain (Sanderson 1988; Samuel 2008). This chapter concentrates on Tantra as a form of yoga; the scriptures, ritual, schools and philosophy of the Tantric traditions are treated in full in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama. It comes before the chapters on the subtle body and on Haṭha Yoga because the vocabulary of both — channels, centres, seed-syllables, the ascent of a power through the body — was first worked out in the Tantras (Section 5.7).

Definition: Tantra

Tantra is a comprehensive spiritual system that views the entire creation as a manifestation of divine energy (Śakti), and employs systematic methods — including mantra, yantra, mudrā, nyāsa, pūjā, and meditation — to realise the ultimate identity of the individual self with the Supreme Reality (Śiva-Śakti).

Many (though not all) Tantric traditions affirm that the world is a manifestation of the divine and that liberation — and worldly powers (siddhi) — can be attained through the body and the senses rather than by fleeing from them. Several Tantras (for example the Buddhist Hevajra Tantra) state the principle that the very things by which the ignorant are bound become, in skilful hands, the means of liberation.

docs.title: 5.2 Historical Development of Tantra
docs.text:
Scholars debate how far Tantra draws on older Vedic, ascetic and goddess cults; what is clear is that it emerged as a distinct, text-based movement around the 5th–6th century CE, the date of the earliest surviving Śaiva Tantra, the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā (Table 5.1) (Sanderson 2009).

Table 5.1. Historical Development of the Tantra Tradition Period Development Background (before c. 500 CE) Vedic ritual and mantra (Atharvaveda); Pāśupata and other Śaiva ascetic orders; goddess cults; Sāṃkhya cosmology Early Tantric (c. 500–900 CE) Earliest Śaiva Tantras (Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā); Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās; Buddhist Tantras (Mahāvairocana); Kaula and goddess-centred (Kulā) traditions Mature Tantric (c. 900–1300 CE) Kashmiri non-dual Śaivism: Vasugupta (c. 850), Somānanda, Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016); Śrīvidyā texts (c. 10th–11th c.); Śaiva Siddhānta in South India; Buddhist Yoginī Tantras Late Tantric (c. 1300–1800 CE) Integration with Haṭha Yoga; Bengali Śākta traditions; Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa (1577); Mahānirvāṇa Tantra (late 18th c.) Modern (19th c. onwards) Rāmakṛṣṇa’s Tantric training; Sir John Woodroffe’s translations; Western “neo-Tantra”

docs.title: 5.3.1 Śiva and Śakti: The Divine Dyad
docs.text:
At the heart of Tantric philosophy lies the doctrine of Śiva-Śakti — the inseparable unity of consciousness (Śiva) and energy (Śakti). Śiva is the static, transcendent principle of pure awareness; Śakti is the dynamic, immanent principle of creative power. They are not two separate realities but two aspects of one Supreme Reality, like fire and its heat, the sun and its light, a word and its meaning (Figure 5.1).

Saundaryalaharī 1

śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavituṃ na ced evaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditum api Only if united with Śakti can Śiva create. Without Her, He cannot even stir.

Figure 5.1. The union of Śiva and Śakti, represented by interlocking triangles — the foundational principle of the Śrī Yantra.

docs.title: 5.3.2 The 36 Tattvas of Śaiva Tantra
docs.text:
While the Sāṃkhya system enumerates 25 tattvas (principles of existence), the Śaiva Tantric tradition expands this to 36 tattvas, adding eleven above the Sāṃkhya schema: five “pure” tattvas, Māyā, and the five “sheaths” (kañcukas) — limited agency (kalā), limited knowledge (vidyā), attachment (rāga), time (kāla) and causal restriction (niyati) — which explain how infinite consciousness appears as a finite, embodied individual (Table 5.2).

Table 5.2. The 36 Tattvas of Śaiva Tantra (Summary) Category Tattvas Description Śuddha (Pure) 1–5 Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddha Vidyā Māyā and the sheaths 6–11 Māyā and the five Kañcukas (limiting powers) Aśuddha (Impure) 12–36 The 25 Sāṃkhya tattvas, from Puruṣa and Prakṛti down to the five gross elements

docs.title: 5.4 Tantric Methods and Practices
docs.text: Tantra employs a wide range of practices. The most common — shared by almost all Tantric traditions — are mantra, yantra or maṇḍala, nyāsa, worship, initiation and meditation; the controversial “five Ms” of some Śākta lineages are discussed separately below.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Mantra
docs.text: Mantra is the foundation of all Tantric practice. Every deity, every yantra, every ritual is activated by its specific mantra. The Tantric understanding of mantra goes beyond mere repetition — the mantra is viewed as the sound body of the deity, identical with the deity itself.

docs.title: 5.4.2 Yantra
docs.text:
A yantra is a geometric diagram that represents the energy pattern of a deity or cosmic principle. It is the visual counterpart of a mantra. The best-known yantra is the Śrī Yantra (also called Śrī Cakra), which represents the goddess Lalitā Tripurasundarī and the entire process of cosmic creation and dissolution (Figure 5.2).

Figure 5.2. Schematic drawing of the Śrī Yantra: the square enclosure (bhūpura) with its four gates, three circles, the sixteen- and eight-petalled lotuses, and nine interlocking triangles, four upward (Śiva) and five downward (Śakti), around the central point (bindu). The triangles are not drawn to exact proportion.

docs.title: 5.4.3 Nyāsa
docs.text: Nyāsa (literally “placing”) is the ritual practice of placing mantras on different parts of the body through touch and visualisation. It transforms the physical body into a sacred vessel, identifying each limb and organ with a specific deity or cosmic principle.

docs.title: 5.4.4 Pūjā (Worship)
docs.text: Tantric worship (pūjā) is an elaborate ritual in which the deity is invoked through mantras, honoured with offerings, and meditated upon. The worship may be external (bāhya pūjā) using physical implements, or internal (āntara pūjā) performed entirely within the practitioner’s consciousness.

docs.title: 5.4.5 Dīkṣā (Initiation)
docs.text: Dīkṣā (initiation) is essential in the Tantric path. Without proper initiation from a qualified Guru (ācārya), Tantric practices are considered ineffective and potentially dangerous. The Guru transmits the mantra, awakens the disciple’s inner Śakti, and provides the necessary guidance for the spiritual journey.

docs.title: 5.5 Śrī Vidyā: The Supreme Knowledge
docs.text: Śrī Vidyā (“the auspicious knowledge”) centres on the worship of the Goddess as Lalitā Tripurasundarī (“the beautiful one of the three cities”) through the Śrī Yantra and the fifteen-syllabled mantra (pañcadaśī), which is divided into three sections (kūṭa); its inner worship identifies the circuits of the yantra with the worshipper’s own body (Volume 6). Śrīvidyā emerged as a distinct tradition around the 10th–11th centuries, with texts such as the Vāmakeśvarīmata and Yoginīhṛdaya, and later became closely associated with the Śaṅkarācārya monasteries of South India, where it was reshaped in a more orthodox, “right-hand” form. Tradition credits Śaṅkara with the Saundaryalaharī, a hymn of 100 verses praising the Goddess through Śrīvidyā symbolism, but most scholars regard the hymn as considerably later than Śaṅkara (Brooks 1992).

docs.title: 5.6 Kashmiri Śaivism: The Crown of Tantric Philosophy
docs.text: Kashmiri Śaivism (an umbrella term for the Trika, Krama, Spanda and Pratyabhijñā traditions) is the most philosophically developed form of Tantric thought. It was worked out in Kashmir between the 9th and 11th centuries by Vasugupta (c. 850), Somānanda (early 10th century), Utpaladeva (10th century) and above all Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016) and his pupil Kṣemarāja, and it presents a non-dual (advaita) vision of reality in which everything is a manifestation of Śiva-consciousness, endowed with absolute freedom (svātantrya) and with reflexive self-awareness (vimarśa). Three of its ideas matter for yoga. Liberation is a “recognition” (pratyabhijñā) that one’s own self is Śiva, not a state produced by technique. Consciousness is not static but vibrates (spanda), so that moments of intense feeling or of transition can open onto it — the basis of the Vijñāna Bhairava’s methods described below. And awakening can be given by grace, in the “descent of power” (śaktipāta) at initiation, which later teachers equated with the awakening of kuṇḍalinī (Chapter 6). Its philosophy is treated in Volume 6.

docs.title: 5.7 Yoga in the Śaiva Scriptures
docs.text:
Much of what later became Haṭha Yoga’s vocabulary — the channels and centres of the subtle body, the fixations on the elements, the seed-syllables, the ascent of a power through the body — was first worked out in the Śaiva Tantras of the second half of the first millennium (Chapters 6 and 7). The structure of these scriptures, with yoga as one of their four “feet” alongside doctrine, ritual and conduct, is described in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama; this section looks at the yoga itself.

Six limbs, not eight. The yoga of the Śaiva scriptures is usually “six-limbed” (ṣaḍaṅga): breath-control, withdrawal of the senses, meditation, fixation, reasoning (tarka) and absorption, though the order varies between texts. The same six, without Patañjali’s ethical limbs and without āsana as a limb, are already listed in the Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad (6.18), and a six-limbed yoga, with partly different limbs, was also taught in the Buddhist Kālacakra tradition (Chapter 9, Section 9.10). The distinctive limb is tarka, which in this context is not logical argument but a discerning judgement of what is to be rejected and what is to be sought; Abhinavagupta, who held that yoga is subordinate to gnosis (jñāna), singled it out in the fourth chapter of his Tantrāloka as the highest of the limbs, because it bears directly on understanding (Vasudeva 2004).

Fixations on the elements. The most characteristic Tantric technique is a series of dhāraṇās in which the yogin fixes the mind, and often the breath, in regions of the body correlated with the five elements, each visualised with its own shape, colour, seed-syllable and presiding deity. Mastery of each fixation is said to give power over its element: the yogin who masters earth cannot be harmed by it, and so on. Such fixations are taught in the earliest surviving Śaiva Tantra, the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā (its oldest parts 5th–6th century), in its book on yoga, the Nayasūtra (Goodall 2015). Birch has pointed out that most Haṭha texts understand dhāraṇā in this Tantric sense, as holding the breath in the body’s elemental regions, rather than in Patañjali’s sense of binding the mind to a place; the five dhāraṇā mudrās of the Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā are a late form of the same practice (Birch 2011).

The conquest of the levels of reality. In the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the root scripture of the Trika on which Abhinavagupta based his Tantrāloka, yoga is a graded ascent through the thirty-six tattvas (Table 5.2). The yogin conquers the elements one by one, then the senses and the mental faculties, experiencing each level of reality from within until he reaches Śiva. Somadeva Vasudeva, who edited the text’s chapters on yoga, has shown that the Mālinīvijayottara does not teach one system but integrates several competing yogas — of the six limbs, of the conquest of the realities, of meditations on the “targets” (lakṣya) of attention — into a single hierarchy (Vasudeva 2004).

Powers and liberation. The Śaiva Tantras distinguished two kinds of initiate: one who seeks liberation and one, the sādhaka, who seeks supernatural powers and enjoyments in this life and in higher worlds. Yoga served both, and the scriptures describe powers — flight, invisibility, entering other bodies — as frankly as the Mahābhārata did (Chapter 1, Section 1.5). For the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, liberation came through initiation, which removes the bonds of the soul, rather than through yoga, which therefore remained an auxiliary. In the non-dualist Trika the emphasis moved from technique to recognition: the highest of Abhinavagupta’s ways, the “way of Śiva” (śāmbhavopāya), works through a sudden intuition rather than through technique, and yoga with its limbs belongs to the lowest of his ways, the “individual” way (āṇavopāya) (Sanderson 1988, 2009).

Vaiṣṇava Tantra. The Pāñcarātra saṃhitās contain comparable chapters on yoga, combining Patañjali’s limbs with breath-control in the nāḍīs and with meditation on the forms of Viṣṇu (Volume 6). Together with the Purāṇic teachings described in Chapter 1 (Section 1.5.3), they explain why the earliest text to teach a yoga it calls Haṭha, the Dattātreyayogaśāstra, could be a Vaiṣṇava work.

Three points follow for the history of Yoga. First, the six-limbed scheme was at least as widespread in the first millennium as Patañjali’s eight, and the early Haṭha texts sometimes follow it: the Vivekamārtaṇḍa teaches six limbs (Chapter 7, Section 7.3.2). Secondly, the Tantric yoga of the scriptures was embedded in initiation, ritual and mantra; when the Haṭha texts presented their techniques as open to anyone without initiation, they were breaking with that setting. Thirdly, the modern picture of a single “Tantric yoga” of seven cakras and kuṇḍalinī, examined in the next chapter, is a late simplification of a literature that taught many different systems.

docs.title: 5.8 Tamil Śaiva Yoga: Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram
docs.text:
The Śaiva yoga of the Sanskrit Tantras has a Tamil counterpart that is still recited in temples. The Tirumantiram (“Sacred Mantra”) of Tirumūlar, a work of about three thousand quatrains arranged in nine sections called tantirams, forms the tenth book of the Tamil Śaiva canon, the Tirumuṟai. Its date is disputed. Hagiography makes Tirumūlar a yogin from the north who entered the body of a dead cowherd, Mūlaṉ, and remained in the Tamil country for three thousand years, composing one verse a year; modern scholars have placed the work anywhere between the sixth and the twelfth centuries, and it may contain layers of different dates (Zvelebil 1973; Ganapathy 1993).

Its third section teaches an eight-limbed yoga whose limbs bear Patañjali’s names but whose content is Tantric: breath-control in the channels, the fixation of the mind in centres of the body, the rousing of an inner fire, the drinking of the nectar that flows from the head, and the eight great powers that follow from mastery. One verse defends the body as the instrument of liberation: if the body perishes, the poet says, the life within it perishes too, and true knowledge is never reached; so, having learnt the means of fostering the body, he fostered the body and with it the life. The concern with a perfected, long-lived body anticipates the Haṭha texts by centuries (Chapter 7). Other sections expound the Śaiva Siddhānta categories of the Lord, the soul and its bonds (pati, paśu, pāśa), ritual, mantra and right conduct, and the work is the source of the line, often quoted as a summary of Tamil Śaivism, that only the ignorant say love and Śiva are two.

Later lists count Tirumūlar among the eighteen Siddhas (Cittar) of Tamil tradition, whose poetry of yoga, alchemy and protest is discussed with the vernacular yoga literature in Chapter 7 (Section 7.16). The Tirumantiram thus stands where three histories meet: the Sanskrit Śaiva Tantras, the Tamil devotional canon, and the Siddha tradition of medicine and immortality treated in Volume 13, Āyurveda.

docs.title: 5.9 The Tantric Textual Tradition
docs.text: The Tantric corpus is vast: the Śaiva Āgamas and Bhairava Tantras, the Śākta Tantras (among them the Kulārṇava), the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās, the works of the Kashmiri Śaiva exegetes and the Buddhist Tantras. Its classification and contents are surveyed in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama. Two works matter especially for the history of Tantric yoga.

docs.title: 5.9.1 The Tantrāloka of Abhinavagupta
docs.text: The Tantrāloka (“Light on the Tantras”), composed by Abhinavagupta around the beginning of the eleventh century, is the most comprehensive work of the non-dual Śaiva tradition. In 37 chapters and some 5,800 verses it sets out theology, ritual and yoga on the basis of the Mālinīvijayottara, and its hierarchy of “ways” (upāya), described above, places the yoga of breath and fixation at the lowest level and sudden recognition at the highest.

docs.title: 5.9.2 The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra — 112 Meditation Techniques
docs.text:
The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra (probably 7th–9th century, from the Trika milieu of Kashmir) is among the most accessible and practically oriented Tantric texts. Cast as a dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess, it presents 112 dhāraṇās (concentration techniques), each offering a distinct doorway into the experience of non-dual consciousness (Singh 1979) (Table 5.3).

Table 5.3. Selected Dhāraṇās from the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra (paraphrased) Technique Method Breath awareness Focus on the points where the in-breath and out-breath arise and turn; in that gap, consciousness reveals itself Moments of intensity At the beginning or end of a sneeze, in fear, grief or surprise, the mind is momentarily emptied — abide in that state Desire contemplation When desire arises, fix attention on it; freed from its object, its energy reveals itself as Śakti Sky meditation Gaze at the clear sky without thought; the mind dissolves into boundless space Music absorption While enjoying song and music, become absorbed in it so completely that the mind is one with it

Scholarly Note: The Vijñāna Bhairava and Modern Meditation

The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra has become popular in modern meditation circles, partly through Paul Reps’s Zen Flesh, Zen Bones (which included a free rendering of it) and through Osho (Rajneesh), whose lectures on its 112 techniques were published as The Book of Secrets. Its emphasis on finding meditative awareness in ordinary moments — eating, listening to music, even sneezing — resonates with modern interest in “everyday” meditation, although the text’s own setting is Tantric Śaiva theology and initiation.

docs.title: 5.10 Transgression, the “Five Ms” and Their Reinterpretation
docs.text:
Popular presentations of Tantra tend either to reduce it to sexuality or, in reaction, to deny that sex and transgression had any place in it. Neither is accurate. Most Tantric ritual was concerned with initiation, mantra, worship and meditation, and the mainstream Śaiva Siddhānta was ritually conservative. But a significant strand — the Kaula and related “left-hand” (vāmācāra) traditions — deliberately used substances and acts that orthodox Brahmanism held to be impure, in order to transcend the distinction between pure and impure and to gain power and liberation (Sanderson 1988; White 2003).

The best-known expression of this is the pañca-makāra or “five Ms” (also called the pañca-tattva), named after the initial letter of each element (Table 5.4).

Table 5.4. The Five Ms (Pañca-makāra) of Left-Hand Śākta Ritual Element Literal meaning Notes Madya Wine Alcohol, forbidden to brahmins in orthodox law Māṃsa Meat Including meats held to be especially impure Matsya Fish Mudrā Parched grain Interpreted in some texts as a hand gesture, and in some modern accounts as the female ritual partner Maithuna Sexual union Ritual intercourse, in some lineages with a partner of low caste, to overcome notions of purity

These elements were used literally in Kaula rites; Abhinavagupta’s Tantrāloka (ch. 29) describes the Kula ritual, including its sexual component, and texts such as the Kulārṇava Tantra prescribe the five elements while warning that they are only for the properly initiated. Over time three responses developed. “Right-hand” (dakṣiṇācāra) practitioners used substitutes (pratinidhi) — milk or coconut water for wine, vegetables or pulses for meat and fish, and the worship of a deity with flowers in place of sexual union. Others internalised the elements as yogic processes: “wine” as the nectar flowing from the head in khecarī mudrā, “meat” as the tongue, “union” as the meeting of kuṇḍalinī with Śiva. And in the colonial period, defenders such as Woodroffe stressed the symbolic readings in response to missionary and Orientalist attacks on Tantra as immoral (Urban 2003).

All three — literal, substitute and internalised — are part of the history. Describing the five Ms only as “symbolic” sanitises that history; describing Tantra only through them distorts it. The ultimate aim professed by all Tantric schools is liberation and the realisation of one’s identity with the divine, alongside the pursuit of worldly powers that many Tantras openly promised.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Kuṇḍalinī, Cakras, and Nāḍīs
docs.text:
Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā 3.1

saśaila-vana-dhātrīṇāṃ yathādhāro'hināyakaḥ sarveṣāṃ yoga-tantrāṇāṃ tathādhāro hi kuṇḍalī Just as the serpent-king (Ananta) supports the earth with its mountains and forests, so Kuṇḍalinī is the support of all Yoga practices.

docs.title: 6.1 The Subtle Body (Sūkṣma Śarīra)
docs.text:
The Tantras described in the last chapter located their deities, mantras and powers within the practitioner’s own body, and in doing so they mapped a body of channels, centres and an inner power that the Haṭha texts of the next chapter took over and made the object of physical technique. This chapter describes that “subtle body”. Vedānta and many later Yoga texts place it within a scheme of three bodies (Table 6.1).

Table 6.1. The Three Bodies (Trividha Śarīra) Body Sanskrit Description Gross Body Sthūla Śarīra The physical body made of the five elements Subtle Body Sūkṣma Śarīra The energy body comprising prāṇa, nāḍīs, cakras, and the mind Causal Body Kāraṇa Śarīra The seed body of latent impressions; the ānandamaya kośa

Tantric and Haṭha texts describe within the subtle body a network of channels (nāḍīs), centres (cakras), and the dormant power known as kuṇḍalinī. This “subtle body” is best understood as a map used in visualisation and meditation, developed over many centuries and in many versions, rather than as a single fixed anatomy (Samuel and Johnston 2013; White 1996).

docs.title: 6.2 The Nāḍī System
docs.text:
The word nāḍī is derived from the Sanskrit root naḍ (to flow). Nāḍīs are the subtle channels through which prāṇa (vital energy) flows throughout the body. They are not identical with the physical nerves or blood vessels but correspond to an energetic anatomy that underlies and interpenetrates the gross body.

The Śiva Saṃhitā gives the number of nāḍīs as 350,000; most other texts give 72,000 (dvāsaptati sahasrāṇi). Of these, fourteen are considered principal, and of the fourteen, three are the most important (Figure 6.1; Table 6.2).

Figure 6.1. The Three Principal Nāḍīs: Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā, shown with the seven Cakras. As in the familiar modern diagram, iḍā and piṅgalā cross at each centre and end at the ājñā; the texts describe their course in different ways. Table 6.2. The Three Principal Nāḍīs Nāḍī Position Quality Energy Characteristics Iḍā Left of spine Lunar (candra) Cooling, calming Ends at the left nostril; associated with the Gaṅgā Piṅgalā Right of spine Solar (sūrya) Heating, activating Ends at the right nostril; associated with the Yamunā Suṣumnā Central (spine) Neutral (agni) Spiritual fire The royal path; kuṇḍalinī rises through it

The Śāṇḍilya and Darśana Upaniṣads and the Yogayājñavalkya name fourteen principal nāḍīs: besides suṣumnā, iḍā and piṅgalā, they list gāndhārī, hastijihvā, pūṣā, yaśasvinī, alambusā, kuhū, śaṅkhinī, payasvinī, vāruṇī, viśvodarā and sarasvatī. The texts agree that these run to the eyes, ears, mouth, tongue, genitals and anus or pervade the body, but they differ over which channel goes where, so no single table can be given.

docs.title: 6.3 The Seven Cakras
docs.text:
The cakras (literally “wheels”) are centres located along the suṣumnā nāḍī, used as supports for visualisation and for the installation of mantras and deities. They are described as lotus-like formations (padma) with varying numbers of petals, each associated with specific syllables, elements and deities. The number of cakras varies between texts: early Buddhist Tantras teach four, many Śaiva texts five, six or more, and some as many as twelve or sixteen. The six-plus-one model presented below became standard only through the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa of Pūrṇānanda (1577) and its English translation by Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe) in The Serpent Power (1919) (Avalon 1974; Leland 2016) (Figure 6.2).

Figure 6.2. The six cakras and the sahasrāra with their bīja mantras, elements, deities and locations, following the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa. Each lotus is drawn in the colour the text gives it (Table 6.3), not in the modern rainbow sequence. Table 6.3. The Cakras of the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa. The lotus colours are those of the text; the familiar rainbow sequence (red to violet) is a 20th-century Western addition. Cakra Petals Element Bīja Lotus colour Location Mūlādhāra 4 Pṛthvī (Earth) LAM Red Perineum / base of spine Svādhiṣṭhāna 6 Jala (Water) VAM Vermilion Root of the genitals Maṇipūra 10 Agni (Fire) RAM Rain-cloud (dark blue) Navel Anāhata 12 Vāyu (Air) YAM Deep red Heart Viśuddha 16 Ākāśa (Ether) HAM Smoky purple Throat Ājñā 2 Manas (Mind) Oṃ White Between eyebrows Sahasrāra 1000 Beyond — White, luminous Crown of head

docs.title: 6.4 Kuṇḍalinī Śakti: The Coiled Serpent Power
docs.text:
Kuṇḍalinī literally means “the coiled one.” It is described as a dormant spiritual energy lying coiled like a serpent at the base of the spine, in the Mūlādhāra Cakra. When awakened through yogic practice, kuṇḍalinī rises through the suṣumnā nāḍī, piercing each cakra in succession, until it reaches the Sahasrāra (the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown), where it unites with Śiva — the supreme consciousness. This union is the goal of Kuṇḍalinī Yoga.

HYP 3.2

suptā guru-prasādena yadā jāgarti kuṇḍalī tadā sarvāṇi padmāni bhidyante granthayo'pi ca When the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī is awakened by the Guru’s grace, all the lotuses (cakras) and knots (granthis) are pierced.

docs.title: 6.4.1 The Three Granthis (Psychic Knots)
docs.text:
Along the suṣumnā, there are three granthis (knots) that obstruct the upward flow of the breath or kuṇḍalinī. In the HYP (4.70–77) their piercing is associated with the heart, the throat and the space between the eyebrows; modern teachers usually place them as in Table 6.4, whose psychological interpretation in the last two columns is modern.

Table 6.4. The Three Granthis (Psychic Knots) Granthi Location Quality Nature of Bondage Brahma Granthi Mūlādhāra–Svādhiṣṭhāna Tamas Attachment to physical pleasures; inertia; lethargy Viṣṇu Granthi Maṇipūra–Anāhata Rajas Attachment to emotional bonds; ambition; power Rudra Granthi Viśuddha–Ājñā Sattva Attachment to siddhis; spiritual pride; subtle ego

docs.title: 6.4.2 Methods of Awakening Kuṇḍalinī
docs.text:
The Haṭha and Tantric texts name several means of awakening kuṇḍalinī. The Haṭha texts rely on breath-control, the locks and the seals, above all the “stimulation of the power” (śakticcālana, HYP 3.104–123); the Tantras on mantras and deities installed in the centres and on fixation of the mind upon them; and the Śaiva traditions on the guru’s grace, the “descent of power” (śaktipāta) at initiation, which the HYP itself echoes when it says that kuṇḍalinī wakes “by the guru’s grace” (3.2). Modern teachers add devotion and self-enquiry as further, spontaneous routes; these are not found in the classical sources.

Health and Safety Note

The texts insist that these practices be learned only from a competent teacher. Intensive breath retention and kuṇḍalinī practices have been associated in clinical reports with anxiety, dissociation and, in vulnerable people, psychotic episodes. People with a history of psychiatric illness, epilepsy, heart disease or high blood pressure, and pregnant women, should not undertake them without medical advice.

docs.title: 6.5 Detailed Description of Each Cakra
docs.text: The following descriptions follow the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa as translated by Avalon (Avalon 1974); the Tantric background of the cakra system is treated in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama.

docs.title: 6.5.1 Mūlādhāra Cakra (Root Centre)
docs.text:
The Mūlādhāra (“root support”) is the foundation cakra, located at the base of the spine between the anus and the genitals. It is depicted as a four-petalled lotus of crimson colour, bearing the Sanskrit syllables va, śa, ṣa, sa. At its centre is a yellow square representing the earth element (pṛthvī tattva), within which is the bīja mantra LAM (Figure 6.3). The deity is Lord Brahmā with the Śakti Ḍākinī.

This is the seat of the sleeping kuṇḍalinī, coiled three and a half times around the svayambhu liṅga.

Figure 6.3. A modern schematic drawing of the Mūlādhāra cakra: four red petals bearing the syllables va, śa, ṣa and sa, the yellow square of earth and the seed-syllable laṃ. The deities and the coiled kuṇḍalinī described in the text are not shown. Image: Andy Holland (2005), CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 6.5.2 Svādhiṣṭhāna Cakra (Sacral Centre)
docs.text: The Svādhiṣṭhāna (“one’s own abode”) is located in the sacral region. It is a six-petalled lotus of vermilion colour, bearing the syllables ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la. At its centre is a white crescent moon representing the water element (jala tattva), with the bīja mantra VAM. The deity is Lord Viṣṇu with Rākiṇī Śakti.

docs.title: 6.5.3 Maṇipūra Cakra (Solar Plexus)
docs.text: The Maṇipūra (“city of jewels”) is located in the navel region. It is a ten-petalled lotus the colour of a rain-cloud, bearing the syllables ḍa through pha. At its centre is a red inverted triangle representing the fire element (agni tattva), with the bīja mantra RAM. The deity is Lord Rudra with Lākiṇī Śakti.

docs.title: 6.5.4 Anāhata Cakra (Heart Centre)
docs.text:
The Anāhata (“unstruck sound”) is located in the heart region. It is a twelve-petalled lotus of deep red colour, bearing the syllables ka through ṭha. At its centre is a smoke-coloured hexagonal star (two interlocking triangles) representing the air element (vāyu tattva), with the bīja mantra YAM. The deity is Īśa (Śiva) with Kākiṇī Śakti.

This is considered the seat of the individual Self (jīvātman) and the source of the “unstruck sound” (anāhata nāda).

docs.title: 6.5.5 Viśuddha Cakra (Throat Centre)
