The same four names are given in the HYP to the stages of inner sound (Chapter 10). These are textual claims, not observed results.

docs.title: 8.6 Precautions and Guidelines
docs.text:
Key Point: Essential Precautions for Prāṇāyāma

  1. Guru’s guidance — Always learn from a qualified teacher

  2. Gradual progression — Never force the breath; increase duration slowly

  3. Empty stomach — Practise on an empty stomach (several hours after a meal)

  4. Clean environment — A well-ventilated, quiet, clean space

  5. Moderate diet — Mita-āhāra (moderate, sāttvika food)

  6. Regular timing — Best times: brāhma muhūrta (pre-dawn), sunset

  7. Steady posture — Must be seated in a firm, comfortable āsana

  8. No strain — If dizziness, nausea, or headache occurs, stop and rest

docs.title: 8.7 The Relationship Between Breath and Mind
docs.text:
One of the most profound insights of Yoga is the intimate connection between breath and mind. As the HYP declares (2.2): “When the breath is unsteady, the mind is unsteady. When the breath is steady, the mind becomes steady.” This bi-directional relationship means that by controlling the breath, one gains control over the mind, and vice versa.

Modern research supports a more limited version of this insight. Slow, controlled breathing shifts autonomic balance towards parasympathetic activity and can reduce subjective anxiety; evidence for effects on cortisol and on EEG rhythms is less consistent, and many studies are small (Zaccaro et al. 2018).

HYP 4.29

indriyāṇāṃ mano nātho mano-nāthas tu mārutaḥ mārutasya layo nāthaḥ sa layo nādam āśritaḥ The mind is lord of the senses; the breath is lord of the mind; absorption (laya) is lord of the breath, and that absorption rests on the inner sound (nāda).

docs.title: 8.8 Prāṇāyāma in the Textual Tradition
docs.text:
The oldest description of breath-control as a technique of meditation is in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, in the verse that follows its instruction on posture (Chapter 1):

Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.9

prāṇān prapīḍyeha sa yukta-ceṣṭaḥ kṣīṇe prāṇe nāsikayocchvasīta duṣṭāśva-yuktam iva vāham enaṃ vidvān mano dhārayetāpramattaḥ Restraining his breaths here, with his movements controlled, he should breathe out through the nose when the breath is diminished. The wise one should hold the mind attentively, as one holds a chariot yoked to unruly horses.

Here, as in Patañjali, the restraint of the breath serves the restraint of the mind. Table 8.3 summarises how later texts developed the practice.

Table 8.3. Prāṇāyāma in the Major Yoga Texts Text Period Key Teachings on Prāṇāyāma Bhagavad Gītā c. 2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE Prāṇa-apāna offerings; prāṇāyāma as sacrifice (yajña) (4.29) Yoga Sūtras c. 325–425 CE Fourth limb; external, internal and suspended movements regulated by place, time and number; a “fourth” beyond these Yogayājñavalkya c. 13th–14th c. CE Prāṇāyāma with fixation of the breath on the elements in the body; therapeutic applications Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā c. 1450 CE Eight kumbhakas detailed; emphasis on nāḍī purification; signs of success; mitāhāra Śiva Saṃhitā c. 15th c. CE Four stages of practice; retention with bandhas; kuṇḍalinī Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā c. 1700 CE Eight kumbhakas, including sahita and kevala; breathing combined with mantra (sagarbha)

docs.title: 8.9 Patañjali’s Analysis of Prāṇāyāma
docs.text:
Patañjali devotes five sūtras (2.49–2.53) to prāṇāyāma. His definition (2.49, quoted in Section 2.5.4) is striking: once posture is mastered, prāṇāyāma is the interruption (gati-viccheda) of the movement of in-breath and out-breath — a cessation, not a technique of breathing. The next sūtra classifies that cessation:

Yoga Sūtra 2.50

bāhyābhyantara-stambha-vṛttir deśa-kāla-saṃkhyābhiḥ paridṛṣṭo dīrgha-sūkṣmaḥ Prāṇāyāma has external, internal, and suspended movements, regulated by place, time, and number, becoming prolonged and subtle.

Following Vyāsa’s commentary, the three movements are explained in Table 8.4. Note that all three are forms of retention; Vyāsa does not equate bāhya and ābhyantara with exhalation and inhalation, as some modern manuals do.

Table 8.4. Patañjali’s Three Types of Prāṇāyāma Type Sanskrit Description External Bāhya Vṛtti Retention after exhalation; the breath is held outside Internal Ābhyantara Vṛtti Retention after inhalation; the breath is held inside Suspended Stambha Vṛtti Suspension of both movements at once, by a single effort, wherever the breath happens to be

The fourth type of prāṇāyāma described in Sūtra 2.51 is the most significant:

Yoga Sūtra 2.51

bāhyābhyantara-viṣayākṣepī caturthaḥ The fourth (type of prāṇāyāma) transcends the domain of the external and the internal.

Scholarly Note

This enigmatic “fourth prāṇāyāma” has been interpreted by commentators in various ways. Vyāsa understands it as a state that transcends the deliberate regulation of breath entirely — a spontaneous cessation that occurs in deep meditation. It is often compared to the kevala kumbhaka of the Haṭha Yoga tradition. The result of this mastery, Patañjali states in Sūtra 2.52, is that “the covering of light is dissolved” (tataḥ kṣīyate prakāśāvaraṇam) — the veil of ignorance is thinned, and the inner light of the Self becomes visible.

docs.title: 8.10 The Role of Bandhas in Prāṇāyāma
docs.text: The three bandhas or “locks” — the root lock at the perineum (mūla), the abdominal lock that makes the “great bird” of the breath fly up (uḍḍīyāna) and the chin lock (jālandhara) — are described with the other mudrās in Chapter 7 (Table 7.6). In the Haṭha texts they are integral to kumbhaka. The HYP prescribes jālandhara at the end of inhalation and uḍḍīyāna at the end of retention; applied together during kumbhaka (modern teachers call this bandha-traya), the locks are said to force the breath into the suṣumnā and awaken kuṇḍalinī.

docs.title: 8.11 Prāṇāyāma Ratios and Progressive Training
docs.text:
Later texts prescribe ratios of inhalation, retention and exhalation, measured in units (mātrā), and the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad’s 1:4:2 is the best known. Modern teachers usually begin with equal breathing without retention and lengthen the exhalation and then the retention by stages; such schemes are not a training programme, and long retentions should not be attempted without supervision.

Key Point: The Principle of Gradualism (Krama)

All traditional texts emphasise that prāṇāyāma must be developed gradually (śanaiḥ śanaiḥ). Just as a lion tamer gradually tames a wild animal, the yogi must gradually bring the breath under control. Forcing the breath leads to illness, mental disturbance, and even danger. The hallmark of correct practice is that it produces feelings of lightness, clarity, and joy — never strain, dizziness, or agitation.

docs.title: 8.12 Modern Scientific Understanding of Prāṇāyāma
docs.text:
Contemporary research has begun to investigate the physiological effects of controlled breathing. The diagram shows mechanisms that are proposed and partly supported; the outcomes in the top box are hypotheses under study, not established effects of prāṇāyāma (Figure 8.3).

Figure 8.3. Proposed physiological pathways for the effects of slow, controlled breathing.

Key research findings include:

  • Slow breathing (about 6 breaths/minute): Engages the baroreflex and increases heart rate variability (a marker of healthy autonomic regulation); this rate is close to the resonant frequency of the cardiovascular system and is the basis of HRV biofeedback (Lehrer and Gevirtz 2014; Zaccaro et al. 2018).

  • Alternate nostril breathing (Nāḍī Śodhana): Small trials report short-term reductions in blood pressure and anxiety; popular claims that it “balances the hemispheres” of the brain are not established.

  • Humming (as in Bhrāmarī): Weitzberg and Lundberg found that humming increases nasal nitric oxide about fifteen-fold compared with quiet exhalation, probably by improving ventilation of the paranasal sinuses (Weitzberg and Lundberg 2002). Claims of wider cardiovascular benefit do not follow from this finding.

  • Kumbhaka (Breath Retention): Breath-holding produces falling blood oxygen and rising carbon dioxide; it has measurable effects on cerebral blood flow, but prolonged retention carries risks and its long-term effects are poorly studied.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Dhyāna: Meditation and the Stages of Samādhi
docs.text:
Bhagavad Gītā 6.10

yogī yuñjīta satatam ātmānaṃ rahasi sthitaḥ ekākī yata-cittātmā nirāśīr aparigrahaḥ The yogi should constantly engage the mind in meditation, dwelling in solitude, alone, with mind and body controlled, free from expectations and possessiveness.

docs.title: 9.1 The Meaning of Dhyāna
docs.text:
Dhyāna (meditation) is the seventh limb of Patañjali’s Aṣṭāṅga Yoga and a practice common to almost every form of yoga. The word is derived from the Sanskrit root dhyai (to contemplate, to think deeply, to meditate). Patañjali defines it as the unbroken extension of a single cognition towards the object (tatra pratyayaikatānatā dhyānam, YS 3.2), a definition discussed with the other limbs in Chapter 2 (Section 2.5.6). This chapter looks at meditation as a practice: its stages, objects, methods and obstacles, and its place in the Upaniṣadic, Buddhist and Jain traditions.

Through Buddhism, the word dhyāna (Pali jhāna) gave rise to the Chinese Ch'an, the Japanese Zen, and the Korean Sŏn — a measure of how widely Indian meditative vocabulary travelled.

docs.title: 9.2 The Progressive Stages: Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi
docs.text: Patañjali treats concentration, meditation and absorption as one continuum, the three “internal” limbs that together form saṃyama (Chapter 2, Sections 2.5.6–2.5.7). Seen from the side of practice, the difference between them is the steadiness of attention. In concentration the mind is fixed on one point but still wanders and must be brought back; in meditation the stream of attention flows without interruption; in absorption the object alone remains and the sense of a separate meditator fades. Most meditation manuals, Hindu, Buddhist and Jain, describe some such progression from effortful focus to effortless absorption, and most warn that the later stages cannot be forced.

docs.title: 9.3 Meditation in the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā
docs.text:
The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā describes three types of meditation (Table 9.1).

Table 9.1. Three Types of Dhyāna (Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā) Type Name Description Gross (sthūla) Sthūla Dhyāna Meditation on a concrete form (deity, Guru, image) Luminous (jyotis) Jyotir Dhyāna Meditation on inner light; the flame of consciousness Subtle (sūkṣma) Sūkṣma Dhyāna Meditation on kuṇḍalinī, bindu, or formless Brahman

docs.title: 9.4 The Stages of Samādhi
docs.text: The stages of absorption that lie beyond meditation — the cognitive absorptions with and without gross and subtle thought, the truth-bearing insight, the seedless absorption and the “cloud of dharma” that precedes liberation — are set out once, with Patañjali’s sūtras and the commentators’ classification, in Chapter 2 (Section 2.3.6; Figure 2.1). The Haṭha texts, for their part, use samādhi as a synonym of Rāja Yoga, of the “no-mind” state (amanaska) and of the dissolution of the mind in inner sound (Chapters 7 and 10); the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā, which closes its sevenfold path with six kinds of samādhi reached through different techniques, shows how far the term had moved from Patañjali’s analysis.

docs.title: 9.5 Meditation Posture and Environment
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā provides precise instructions for the meditation posture:

Gītā 6.11–6.13

śucau deśe pratiṣṭhāpya sthiram āsanam ātmanaḥ nāty-ucchritaṃ nāti-nīcaṃ cailājina-kuśottaram tatraikāgraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā yata-cittēndriya-kriyaḥ upaviśyāsane yuñjyād yogam ātma-viśuddhaye samaṃ kāya-śiro-grīvaṃ dhārayann acalaṃ sthiraḥ saṃprekṣya nāsikāgraṃ svaṃ diśaś cānavalokayan In a clean spot, having established a firm seat for oneself, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass; thereon, making the mind one-pointed, with thoughts and senses controlled, one should practise Yoga for self-purification, holding the body, head, and neck erect and still, gazing at the tip of the nose, not looking in any direction.

docs.title: 9.6 Yoga Nidrā: Yogic Sleep
docs.text:
Yoga Nidrā (“yogic sleep”) is a state of conscious deep sleep — a systematic method of inducing complete physical, mental, and emotional relaxation while maintaining awareness. It is often described as the state between waking and sleeping, where the body is in deep rest but the mind remains fully alert.

In pre-modern texts yoganidrā denotes either the cosmic sleep of Viṣṇu or, in some Haṭha works, a state of samādhi. The modern guided-relaxation practice of that name was created in the 1960s–70s by Swāmī Satyānanda Sarasvatī of the Bihar School of Yoga, who said he drew upon the Tantric practice of nyāsa (the ritual placing of mantras on different parts of the body) as well as modern relaxation methods.

Key Point: The Practice of Yoga Nidrā

A typical Yoga Nidrā session includes the following stages:

  1. Preparation: Lying in Śavāsana; setting a saṃkalpa (resolve)

  2. Rotation of consciousness: Awareness is guided systematically through each part of the body

  3. Breath awareness: Observation of the natural breath

  4. Opposite sensations: Experience of pairs of opposites (heavy-light, hot-cold)

  5. Visualisation: Guided imagery (nature scenes, symbols, cakras)

  6. Saṃkalpa: Repetition of the resolve

  7. Return: Gradual return to external awareness

Research on Yoga Nidrā is limited. A small brain-imaging study found increased dopamine release in the striatum during the practice (Kjaer et al. 2002), and some trials report reduced anxiety, but larger and better-controlled studies are needed.

docs.title: 9.7 The Four Attitudes (Bhāvanās)
docs.text:
Among Patañjali’s remedies for the obstacles that scatter the mind (Chapter 2, Section 2.3.5), one became a meditation practice in its own right in several traditions: the cultivation of four attitudes (bhāvanās) towards others (Table 9.2):

Yoga Sūtra 1.33

maitrī-karuṇā-muditōpekṣāṇāṃ sukha-duḥkha-puṇyāpuṇya-viṣayāṇāṃ bhāvanātaś citta-prasādanam By cultivating friendliness towards the happy, compassion towards the suffering, joy towards the virtuous, and equanimity towards the non-virtuous — the mind becomes serene.

Table 9.2. The Four Bhāvanās (Attitudes for Mental Serenity), with effects as explained by commentators. The same four are the Buddhist brahmavihāras. Attitude Towards Effect Maitrī (Friendliness) Happy people Removes jealousy Karuṇā (Compassion) Suffering people Removes callousness Muditā (Joy) Virtuous people Removes envy Upekṣā (Equanimity) Non-virtuous people Removes contempt and agitation

docs.title: 9.8 Classification of Meditation Objects in the Yoga Tradition
docs.text:
The Yoga, Tantric and Vedāntic traditions offer a wide range of meditation objects (ālambana), suited to different temperaments and usually graded from gross to subtle; Patañjali himself allows meditation on “whatever one likes” (YS 1.39). Table 9.3 groups the principal objects with their sources.

Table 9.3. Hierarchy of Meditation Objects from Gross to Subtle Category Examples Tradition and Textual Source Places in the body (deśa) Navel circle; heart lotus; light in the head; tip of the nose; tip of the tongue Vyāsa on Yoga Sūtra 3.1 Physical form (Sthūla) Mūrti of the chosen deity (Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī); the guru; flame; yantra; lotus Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.28; Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā 6; Āgama texts Elements and cakras The five elements with their shapes and colours; the cakras with their bījas and deities Tantric and Haṭha texts; Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa Breath (Prāṇa) Inhalation-exhalation cycle; pause between breaths Yoga Sūtras 1.34; Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā Mantra Oṃ; so'ham; personal mantra from Guru Yoga Sūtras 1.27–28; Tantra texts Inner light (Jyotis) Luminous point in the heart or between the eyebrows Yoga Sūtras 1.36; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad Sound (Nāda) Inner sounds heard in meditation; anāhata nāda Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā 4.65–102 Formless awareness Pure consciousness without object; the witness (sākṣin); the enquiry “Who am I?” Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad; Yoga Sūtras 1.51; Advaita (Chapter 4)

docs.title: 9.8.1 The Practice of Antar Trāṭaka — Internal Gazing
docs.text: The Haṭha Yoga tradition describes Trāṭaka (steady gazing) as a powerful bridge between external practice and internal meditation. After gazing steadily at an external object (typically a small mark or, in modern practice, a candle flame) until the eyes water (HYP 2.31), the practitioner closes the eyes; modern teachers add visualisation of the after-image at the ājñā cakra (the point between the eyebrows). This practice develops Ekāgratā (one-pointedness) and prepares the mind for deeper, objectless meditation.

docs.title: 9.9 Dhyāna in the Upaniṣadic Tradition
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads contain some of the earliest and most profound instructions on meditation in any tradition. The progression from the older to the younger Upaniṣads reveals an increasingly systematic understanding of contemplative practice (Table 9.4).

Table 9.4. Meditation Teachings in Major Upaniṣads Upaniṣad Key Meditation Teaching Bṛhadāraṇyaka Neti Neti — the via negativa: meditation by progressively negating all that is not the Self Chāndogya Dāhara Vidyā — meditation on the tiny space within the heart, which contains the entire universe Kaṭha The chariot metaphor: the Ātman as the rider, buddhi as the charioteer, manas as the reins, senses as the horses — meditation as the mastery of this inner vehicle Śvetāśvatara Detailed meditation posture, breath regulation, and visualisation of inner fire and light Māṇḍūkya The four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, Turīya) as progressive stages of meditative realisation

The Śvetāśvatara’s instruction on posture (2.8) is quoted in Chapter 1.

The Dāhara Vidyā — Meditation on the Inner Space

The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.1.3) declares: “As vast as this external space is the space within the heart. Within it are contained both heaven and earth, both fire and wind, both sun and moon, lightning and stars. Whatever is here in the world and whatever is not — all that is contained within the heart.” This Dāhara Vidyā (meditation on the tiny inner space) represents one of the most ancient and profound meditation techniques in the Indian tradition. The practitioner is instructed to contemplate the space within the heart as identical with infinite Brahman — discovering that the microcosm of the individual self contains the entirety of the macrocosm.

docs.title: 9.10 Buddhist and Jain Yoga
docs.text: Brahmanical Yoga was never the only Indian science of meditation. Buddhist and Jain renunciants developed their own disciplines from the time of the Buddha and Mahāvīra, and the three traditions borrowed from, argued with and redefined one another for well over a thousand years (Bronkhorst 1993; Samuel 2008). Their doctrines and institutions are treated in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā; this section outlines their contribution to the history of yoga.

docs.title: 9.10.1 Buddhist Meditation
docs.text:
The early Buddhist discourses (the Pali Nikāyas and their parallels in other languages) describe four meditative absorptions, the jhānas (Sanskrit dhyāna). The first is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (vitakka, vicāra) and by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; in the second, thought falls away and the mind becomes unified; in the third, rapture fades into equanimity and mindfulness; the fourth is beyond pleasure and pain, purified by equanimity. Beyond these lie four formless attainments, from the sphere of infinite space to the sphere of “neither perception nor non-perception”. According to the discourses, the future Buddha learnt the last two from his teachers Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta and found them insufficient; liberation required insight (vipassanā, Sanskrit vipaśyanā) into impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self, joined to calm (samatha, śamatha) (Gethin 1998; Wynne 2007). The Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta organises mindfulness under four headings — body (beginning with the breath), feelings, mind and mental phenomena — and became the charter of later insight meditation.

The parallels with Patañjali are close and long recognised. The first two stages of cognitive samādhi in YS 1.17 bear the Buddhist names vitarka and vicāra; the five qualities that lead to samādhi in YS 1.20 (faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration and insight) are the Buddhist five “faculties”; and the four attitudes of YS 1.33 (Table 9.2) are the Buddhist brahmavihāras. Buddhist scholasticism produced its own manuals of yoga. Buddhaghosa’s Visuddhimagga (5th century) lists forty meditation subjects — coloured and elemental discs (kasiṇa), the foulness of the body, recollections, the four divine abidings and others — and matches them to the temperaments of different students. In North India the school known as Yogācāra (“practitioners of yoga”) took its name from meditative practice, and its vast Yogācārabhūmi maps the stages of the path. The late Buddhist Tantras taught subtle-body practices of their own: the Kālacakra Tantra (early 11th century) teaches a six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) of withdrawal, meditation, breath control, retention, recollection and absorption, and the earliest Haṭha text, the Amṛtasiddhi, comes from a Buddhist milieu (Chapter 7). The Tantras of this class divide practice into a “generation stage” (utpattikrama), in which the practitioner visualises himself as the deity in its maṇḍala, and a “completion stage” (sampannakrama or niṣpannakrama), in which he works directly with the channels, winds and drops (nāḍī, prāṇa, bindu) to bring the winds into the central channel. The completion-stage yogas — among them the “inner heat” (caṇḍālī, Tibetan gtum mo) of the Hevajra Tantra and the cycle later known in Tibet as the Six Yogas of Nāropa — were carried to Tibet from the eleventh century and are still practised there; they are the closest Buddhist relatives of Haṭha Yoga’s aim of forcing the breath into the central channel (Samuel 2008). In the 20th century the Burmese revival of insight meditation, carried to India by S.N. Goenka from 1969, and the secular “mindfulness” programmes derived from it, made Buddhist meditation as global as postural yoga.

docs.title: 9.10.2 Jain Meditation and Jain Yoga
docs.text:
Jain usage is distinctive. In Jain doctrine yoga first means the activity of body, speech and mind through which karmic matter flows into the soul (kāya-vāṅ-manaḥ-karma yogaḥ, Tattvārthasūtra 6.1); the ascetic’s aim is to bring this “yoga” to rest. The early ideal is the motionless standing posture of “abandoning the body” (kāyotsarga) in which Mahāvīra and the Tīrthaṅkaras are portrayed. Umāsvāti’s Tattvārthasūtra defines meditation (dhyāna) as the restraint of thought on a single object (9.27) and distinguishes four kinds: “sorrowful” and “cruel” meditation, which bind, and “virtuous” (dharma) and “pure” (śukla) meditation, which lead to liberation (Dundas 2002).

From the 8th century Jain authors engaged directly with Patañjala Yoga. Haribhadra Sūri wrote several works on yoga, among them the Yogabindu and the Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya, which arranges the path in eight “views” (dṛṣṭi) correlated with Patañjali’s eight limbs and discusses the yogas of other schools with notable generosity (Chapple 2003). Śubhacandra’s Jñānārṇava (11th century) and Hemacandra’s Yogaśāstra (12th century), written for the Caulukya king Kumārapāla, combine the ethics of the Jain layman and monk with breath control and four graded objects of virtuous meditation — the body, syllables and mantras, the form of the Jina, and the formless — while warning that breath control is not needed for liberation and may disturb the mind (Qvarnström 2002). In the 1970s Ācārya Mahāprajña of the Terāpanth order developed Prekṣā Dhyāna, a modern Jain meditation system that draws on these sources.

docs.title: 9.10.3 Shared Ground
docs.text: Across the three traditions the vocabulary of practice — dhyāna, samādhi, bhāvanā, the breath, the four divine attitudes — is largely shared, while the goal is understood differently: the isolation of the self (puruṣa) in Sāṃkhya-Yoga, the extinction of craving and ignorance (nirvāṇa) in Buddhism, and the release of the soul (jīva) from karmic matter in Jainism. Christian contemplative prayer, Sufi murāqaba and Daoist inner alchemy also cultivate inner stillness, and interpret it in their own terms.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Mantra Yoga, Laya Yoga, and Nāda Yoga
docs.text: Part A: Mantra Yoga — The Path of Sacred Sound

docs.title: 10.1 Mantra
docs.text:
Mantra Yoga is the spiritual discipline based on the repetitive chanting or mental recitation of sacred sound formulas (mantras). Grammatically, mantra is formed from the root man (to think) with the instrumental suffix -tra: “an instrument of thought”. Tantric texts add a traditional etymology, mananāt trāyate, “that which protects when it is meditated upon”.

Definition: Mantra

A mantra is a sacred syllable, word, or phrase believed to be endowed with spiritual power (śakti). According to the tradition, when it is repeated with faith, concentration, and proper intonation, it transforms the consciousness of the practitioner, purifies the mind, and leads to the direct experience of the deity or principle that the mantra embodies.

Several Indian traditions treat sound (śabda) as a primordial creative force. The Upaniṣads speak of a “sound-Brahman” (śabda-brahman) to be known before the supreme Brahman (Maitrī Upaniṣad 6.22); the grammarian Bhartṛhari (5th century) identified Brahman with the eternal Word; and the Tantras describe the universe as unfolding from the Goddess as Speech (vāk) through the letters of the alphabet (see Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā). The Vedic tradition is fundamentally an oral tradition, in which the sacred sounds of the Vedas are transmitted with extraordinary precision from Guru to disciple.

docs.title: 10.2 Types of Mantras
docs.text:
Table 10.1 lists the principal kinds of mantra.

Table 10.1. Classification of Mantras Type Description and Examples Bīja Mantras (Seed) Single-syllable mantras containing the essence of a deity or element: Oṃ, Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, Śrīṃ, Aiṃ Vedic Mantras Mantras from the Vedas: Gāyatrī Mantra, Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (ṚV 7.59.12), Śānti Mantras Purāṇic and Āgamic Mantras Formulas of devotional and sectarian worship: Om Namaḥ Śivāya, Om Namo Nārāyaṇāya Tāntric Mantras Complex formulas from the Tantra traditions, often with specific nyāsa rituals Nāma Mantras Divine names: Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Devī

docs.title: 10.2.1 The Praṇava: Oṃ
docs.text:
The supreme mantra of the Yoga tradition is Oṃ (also written AUM), known as the Praṇava. It is the primordial sound from which all creation emerges and into which it dissolves.

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 1

oṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvaṃ tasyopavyākhyānaṃ bhūtaṃ bhavad bhaviṣyad iti sarvam oṃkāra eva yac cānyat trikālātītaṃ tad apy oṃkāra eva Oṃ — this syllable is all this. All that is past, present, and future is Oṃ. And whatever transcends the three times — that too is Oṃ.

The Upaniṣad goes on (verses 8–12) to equate the three constituent sounds A, U and M with the waking, dreaming and deep-sleep states of the self — named Vaiśvānara, Taijasa and Prājña — and the soundless “measureless” syllable with the fourth state, Turīya (see Table 1.5 in Chapter 1). Repetition of Oṃ is thus also a contemplation of the whole range of consciousness.

docs.title: 10.2.2 The Gāyatrī Mantra
docs.text:
The Gāyatrī Mantra (also called the Sāvitrī) is considered the most sacred mantra of the Vedic tradition. The verse itself is Ṛg Veda 3.62.10; the opening om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ (the syllable Oṃ and the three “utterances”, vyāhṛtis) is prefixed in ritual use. Traditionally its recitation was restricted to initiated twice-born men; in the 19th and 20th centuries reform movements such as the Ārya Samāj and many modern teachers opened it to all.

Gāyatrī Mantra — Ṛg Veda 3.62.10, with the ritual prefix

om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt We meditate upon the glorious splendour of the Divine Light (Savitṛ). May that Light illuminate our intellects.

docs.title: 10.3 Methods of Japa (Mantra Repetition)
docs.text:
Japa is the systematic repetition of a mantra. The tradition distinguishes three modes: aloud (vācika), whispered so that the lips move but no sound is heard (upāṃśu), and mental (mānasa). The Manusmṛti (2.85) already ranks them, declaring the sacrifice of muttered prayer ten times better than the prescribed rites, the whispered form a hundred times and the mental a thousand times better; mental japa is accordingly held by the tradition to be the most powerful. Repetitions are usually counted on a rosary (mālā) of 108 beads, and modern devotional practice adds the writing of a mantra many times over (likhita japa). Patañjali’s own instruction on the praṇava concerns meaning as much as sound:

Yoga Sūtra 1.28

taj-japas tad-artha-bhāvanam The repetition of that (Praṇava) and meditation on its meaning (is the practice).

Patañjali emphasises that japa must be accompanied by artha-bhāvanam — deep contemplation of the meaning. Mechanical repetition without awareness yields limited results; it is the union of sound and meaning that produces the transformative power of mantra.

docs.title: 10.4 The Bīja Mantras and the Cakras
docs.text:
In the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa each of the six cakras carries the seed syllable (bīja) of its element — laṃ (earth), vaṃ (water), raṃ (fire), yaṃ (air) and haṃ (space) — with Oṃ at the ājñā; the syllables are installed and meditated upon in the cakras, together with the letters on the petals of each lotus (Table 6.3 in Chapter 6). The psychological “effects” that modern teachers attach to each bīja (grounding, creativity, confidence and so on) are not found in the classical texts.

Part B: Laya Yoga — The Yoga of Dissolution

docs.title: 10.5 The Meaning of Laya
docs.text:
Laya means “dissolution”, “absorption” or “merging”, and layayoga is the yoga in which the mind is dissolved in its object until no separate mind remains. The Haṭha texts define the state precisely:

HYP 4.34

layo laya iti prāhuḥ kīdṛśaṃ laya-lakṣaṇam apunar-vāsanotthānāl layo viṣaya-vismṛtiḥ People say “laya, laya” — but what is the mark of laya? Laya is the forgetting of sense-objects, because latent impressions no longer arise.

In the medieval yoga texts layayoga is one of four yogas, with mantra, haṭha and rāja. The Dattātreyayogaśāstra and the Amaraughaprabodha arrange the four in a hierarchy of practitioners, in which laya stands above mantra and below haṭha and rāja (Chapter 7, Section 7.3.1), and the Yogabīja makes them successive stages of one “great yoga”. The methods the texts group under laya are varied: fixing the mind on points inside or outside the body, gazes such as the śāmbhavī mudrā, in which the eyes are open but attention is turned inward, and above all listening to the inner sound. The Haṭhapradīpikā says that Ādinātha taught a vast number of methods of laya, but that attention to the inner sound (nādānusandhāna) is the foremost of them (4.66), and it treats laya, the “no-mind” state (amanaska), Rāja Yoga and samādhi as names for one goal (4.3–4) (Birch 2011; Mallinson and Singleton 2017).

docs.title: 10.5.1 The Dissolution of the Elements
docs.text:
A second meaning of laya comes from Tantric ritual. In the rite of purifying the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), which precedes worship in many Tantras, the practitioner dissolves the elements of his body in imagination, each into its subtler source — earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, ether into mind and mind into pure consciousness — and then rebuilds a divine body in which the deity can be worshipped. The ascent of kuṇḍalinī through the cakras, each the seat of an element, was read in the same terms (Chapter 6). The modern presentation of “Laya Yoga” as a systematic dissolution of the elements through the cakras combines this Tantric rite with the medieval yoga of absorption; the classical sources keep them apart.

Part C: Nāda Yoga — The Yoga of Inner Sound

docs.title: 10.6 The Meaning of Nāda
docs.text:
Nāda literally means “sound” or “vibration.” Nāda Yoga is the discipline of attuning to the inner, mystical sound (anāhata nāda — the “unstruck sound”) that arises spontaneously within the body, without any external cause. By following this inner sound deeper and deeper, the mind is drawn inward and eventually dissolves in the supreme silence.

HYP 4.93

sarva-cintāṃ parityajya sāvadhānena cetasā nāda evānusandheyo yoga-sāmrājyam icchatā Abandoning all thoughts, with an attentive mind, one who desires the kingdom of Yoga should concentrate solely on Nāda.

docs.title: 10.7 The Four Stages of Nāda
docs.text:
The Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā (4.69–76) describes four progressive stages as the breath pierces the three knots, each marked by a characteristic inner sound (Table 10.2).

Table 10.2. The Four Stages of Nāda (Inner Sound) Stage Name Description of the Sound 1 Ārambha (Beginning) Brahma granthi pierced; tinkling of ornaments heard in the space of the heart 2 Ghaṭa (Pot) Viṣṇu granthi pierced; the breath enters the middle channel; the sound of a kettledrum in the throat 3 Paricaya (Familiarity) The sound of a drum (mardala) in the space between the eyebrows 4 Niṣpatti (Consummation) Rudra granthi pierced; sounds of flute and vīṇā; the state of Rāja Yoga

Elsewhere in the same chapter (4.85–86) the HYP describes the sounds heard as practice deepens: at first loud sounds like the ocean, thunder and kettledrums; in the middle, drums, conch and bells; at the end, tinkling bells, flute, vīṇā and the humming of bees.

docs.title: 10.8 The Practice of Nāda Yoga
docs.text:
The HYP’s instructions are brief. The yogin sits in the “liberated” posture (muktāsana), adopts the inward gaze of śāmbhavī mudrā and listens to the sound in the right ear (4.67); later teachers add the closing of the ears, eyes and mouth with the fingers (ṣaṇmukhī mudrā). At first loud, external-seeming sounds are heard, then subtler ones; the mind, the text says, is drawn to the subtlest sound as a bee to nectar and dissolves in it, and when even that sound ceases the yogin is in samādhi.

The doctrine of inner sound did not stay within the yoga texts. The Sants and the Sikh Gurus spoke of the “unstruck” sound (anahad) as the sign of the divine name realised within (Chapter 7, Section 7.17). Musicians took it over too. Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara (13th century), the most influential Sanskrit treatise on music, opens its account of musical sound with a description of the body and its centres and derives audible sound (āhata) from the meeting of breath and the body’s fire, beside the unstruck sound (anāhata) of the yogins; “Nāda Yoga” is still the name by which Indian musicians describe their discipline (Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya).

docs.title: 10.9 The Principal Bīja Mantras
docs.text:
The Bīja Mantras (seed syllables) represent the most concentrated form of sacred sound. Each Bīja is understood not as a word with lexical meaning but as a sonic essence — a vibrational pattern that directly embodies the energy of a specific cosmic principle or deity (Table 10.3).

Table 10.3. Major Bīja Mantras and Their Deities (the cakra assignments reflect modern teaching and vary between sources) Bīja Deity/Principle Cakra Significance Oṃ Brahman (the Absolute) Sahasrāra The source of all mantras; the praṇava Hrīṃ Māyā Śakti Anāhata The heart bīja; veiling and revealing power Śrīṃ Lakṣmī Maṇipūra Abundance, auspiciousness, prosperity Klīṃ Kāmadeva / Kṛṣṇa Svādhiṣṭhāna Desire, attraction, creative energy Aiṃ Sarasvatī Viśuddha Knowledge, speech, learning Hūṃ Śiva / Agni Maṇipūra Destruction of obstacles; fierce protective energy Krīṃ Kālī Mūlādhāra Transformative power; dissolution of bondage Gaṃ Gaṇeśa Mūlādhāra Removal of obstacles; auspicious beginnings

Tantric texts give many of these syllables traditional names. Oṃ is the praṇava, regarded as the seed from which all others emerge; Hrīṃ is the “seed of Māyā” or of Bhuvaneśvarī; Klīṃ the “seed of desire” (kāmabīja); Śrīṃ the seed of Śrī or Lakṣmī; and Aiṃ the “seed of speech” (vāgbīja), sacred to Sarasvatī.

In the ritual use of a mantra, the kīlaka (“pin”) is a component said to “lock” its power, which is released by proper initiation. The ending in nasal resonance (anusvāra, ṃ) is interpreted in Tantric theory as the bindu; claims that bījas have been shown to have specific physiological effects are not supported by research.

docs.title: 10.10 Mantra and the Guru-Śiṣya Paramparā
docs.text:
In the traditional understanding, a mantra is not effective merely by being read from a book or heard casually. It must be received through Dīkṣā (initiation) from a qualified Guru who stands in an unbroken lineage (Paramparā) of transmission. The Guru imparts not merely the sound but the caitanya (consciousness-energy) of the mantra, awakened through his or her own practice (Table 10.4).

Table 10.4. Stages of Mantra Transmission and Practice Stage Sanskrit Term Description Initiation Dīkṣā The Guru transmits the mantra with its specific svara (intonation), nyāsa (ritual placement), and dhyāna-śloka (meditation verse) Preliminary practice Puraścaraṇa The practitioner completes the prescribed number of repetitions (often 100,000 per syllable of the mantra) to “awaken” the mantra Matured practice Mantra Siddhi Through sustained practice, the mantra becomes spontaneously active in the practitioner’s consciousness, arising without effort Integration Ajāpā Japa The mantra merges with the breath and continues spontaneously, even during sleep

Scholarly Note: The Concept of Mantra Caitanya

The concept of Mantra Caitanya — the “aliveness” or “awakened consciousness” of a mantra — is central to the Tantric understanding of sacred sound. A mantra without Caitanya is compared to a seed that has been roasted: it retains its external form but has lost the capacity to sprout. The Guru’s role in Dīkṣā is held to be precisely to transmit this living energy, which has been maintained through an unbroken chain of teacher-to-student transmission extending, in principle, back to the original Ṛṣi who first “heard” the mantra in deep meditation.

docs.title: 10.11 The Integration of Mantra, Laya, and Nāda
docs.text: Mantra Yoga, Laya Yoga, and Nāda Yoga are intimately related. Mantra provides the external vehicle of sound; Laya provides the process of progressive dissolution; and Nāda provides the inner guide that leads the mind to its final dissolution in the Absolute. Together, they constitute a path of liberation through sound — from the grossest audible chant to the subtlest inaudible vibration, and finally, in the tradition’s own terms, to the silence beyond all sound, which is Brahman itself (compare HYP 4.5, quoted in Chapter 7).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Yoga in the Modern World: Global Spread and Contemporary Debates
docs.text:
Bhagavad Gītā 6.46

tapasvibhyo'dhiko yogī jñānibhyo'pi mato'dhikaḥ karmibhyaś cādhiko yogī tasmād yogī bhavārjuna The yogi is superior to the ascetic, superior even to the person of knowledge, and superior to the one who performs ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, be a yogi.

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction: Yoga’s Journey Across the World
docs.text:
In the last 130 years Yoga has travelled further than at any time in its long history. Practised in some form on every continent, taught in studios, hospitals, schools and prisons, and promoted by the Government of India and the United Nations, it has become one of India’s most visible contributions to world culture.

This success raises questions that this chapter tries to answer honestly. What exactly travelled? Modern “yoga” — for most people a class of postures and breathing — differs greatly from the meditative discipline of Patañjali and from the secret ascetic techniques of medieval Haṭha Yoga. How did the modern form come about? What does scientific research actually show about its health effects? And what has been the cost of the guru model when it has been transplanted into commercial settings? The chapter considers the modern masters, the history of modern postural yoga, the televised mass yoga of contemporary India, the abuse scandals that have shaken several lineages, the state of the research evidence, and the politics, institutions and debates of the present.

docs.title: 11.2.1 The United Nations Resolution
docs.text:
On 11 December 2014, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 69/131, declaring 21 June the International Day of Yoga (IDY). The resolution, proposed by India, was co-sponsored by 177 member states — a record for a General Assembly resolution of its kind at the time — and adopted without a vote.

The initiative was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his address to the General Assembly on 27 September 2014. The date chosen, 21 June, is the summer solstice, the longest day of the year in the northern hemisphere.

Note: Resolution 69/131 — Key Facts

  • Date of Adoption: 11 December 2014

  • Resolution Number: A/RES/69/131

  • Co-sponsors: 177 member states

  • Day Designated: 21 June, International Day of Yoga

  • First Observance: 21 June 2015

  • Adoption Method: Without a vote

docs.title: 11.2.2 The First International Day of Yoga: 21 June 2015
docs.text:
The inaugural International Day of Yoga on 21 June 2015 was marked by events around the world. In New Delhi, a mass session on Rajpath (now Kartavya Path), led by the Prime Minister, set Guinness World Records for the largest yoga session (nearly 36,000 participants) and the most nationalities taking part (Figure 11.1). India Post marked the day with a commemorative stamp. The Ministry of AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy) has since coordinated IDY through Indian missions abroad.

The Common Yoga Protocol (CYP), drawn up by a panel of yoga experts convened by the Ministry, provides a sequence of about 45 minutes of āsana, prāṇāyāma and meditation intended for people of all ages, and has been the basis of IDY events in many countries. In December 2016 UNESCO inscribed Yoga on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Figure 11.1. The first International Day of Yoga, 21 June 2015: participants seated in rows along Rajpath, New Delhi, with large screens relaying the address. Photo: Ministry of Ayush, GODL-India, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.text:
Figure 11.2 marks the main events, from Vivekānanda’s Chicago address to the WHO mYoga app.

Figure 11.2. Timeline of Yoga’s Global Spread (1893–2021).

docs.title: 11.4 The Great Modern Masters
docs.text: The global spread of Yoga is inseparable from a succession of teachers who, from the late nineteenth century, reimagined its transmission for a new age; Mark Singleton and Ellen Goldberg’s collection Gurus of Modern Yoga studies many of them (Singleton and Goldberg 2014).

docs.title: 11.4.1 Swāmī Vivekānanda (1863–1902)
docs.text:
Born Narendranath Datta in Calcutta, Vivekānanda became the foremost disciple of Rāmakṛṣṇa. His address to the Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago on 11 September 1893 made him famous, and his lectures in the United States and Britain introduced Western audiences to Rāja, Karma, Bhakti and Jñāna Yoga.

Key Point: Vivekānanda’s Key Contributions

  • Published Rāja Yoga (1896), a highly influential English presentation of Patañjali’s Yoga (Vivekananda 1896)

  • Founded the Vedanta Society of New York (1894) and the Ramakrishna Mission (1897)

  • Presented Yoga as a universal “science” open to people of any religion

  • Promoted “practical Vedānta” — spirituality joined to social service

Vivekānanda’s Yoga was meditative and philosophical. He was openly dismissive of Haṭha Yoga, which he regarded as mere physical culture of little spiritual value — a reminder that the posture-centred yoga that later became global was not what the first modern ambassador of Yoga taught (De Michelis 2004; Singleton 2010).

docs.title: 11.4.2 Paramahansa Yogananda (1893–1952)
docs.text: Yogananda brought Kriyā Yoga — a technique of breath control and meditation transmitted, according to his lineage, from Mahāvatār Bābājī through Lāhirī Mahāśaya and Swāmī Sri Yukteswar — to the United States, where he settled in 1920 and founded the Self-Realization Fellowship. His Autobiography of a Yogi (1946) became one of the most widely read spiritual books of the twentieth century.

docs.title: 11.4.3 Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950) and Integral Yoga
docs.text: Aurobindo Ghose, educated at Cambridge, was a leader of the radical wing of the nationalist movement in Bengal until his arrest in the Alipore bomb case of 1908. Acquitted in 1909, he withdrew in 1910 to French Pondicherry, where he devoted the rest of his life to yoga. His “Integral Yoga” (pūrṇa yoga) is set out above all in The Synthesis of Yoga, serialised in his journal Arya between 1914 and 1921 (Aurobindo 1999). Its premise is that each classical yoga develops one part of the human being — Haṭha the body and the life-force, Rāja the mind, the Gītā’s yogas of works, knowledge and devotion the will, the intellect and the heart — and that a synthesis must take them all up. Its goal is not escape from the world, which Aurobindo thought the ascetic traditions had sought, but the transformation of human nature by the descent of a higher, “supramental” consciousness, so that liberation would be embodied and in the end collective. Its method is less a set of techniques than an attitude: aspiration, the rejection of lower impulses and surrender to the divine Śakti, whom his followers saw embodied in his collaborator Mirra Alfassa, “the Mother” (1878–1973), who led the Sri Aurobindo Ashram and founded Auroville in 1968. Peter Heehs’s biography places the teaching in the context of Aurobindo’s reading of the Gītā, the Upaniṣads and the Tantras, and of Western evolutionary thought (Heehs 2008). Aurobindo is the clearest case of a modern teacher who used the many yogas of the tradition to build a new system rather than to restore an old one.

docs.title: 11.4.4 T. Krishnamacharya (1888–1989)
docs.text:
Tirumalai Krishnamacharya is widely regarded as the most influential figure in the making of modern postural yoga. Born in Karnataka, he was a Sanskrit scholar trained in several śāstras; by his own account he studied yoga for seven years with a teacher, Rāmmohan Brahmacārī, in the Himalayas, though this cannot be independently verified.

From 1933 he ran a yogaśālā in the Jaganmohan Palace in Mysore under the patronage of Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV. There he developed a vigorous style that linked āsanas with breath in flowing sequences (vinyāsa) and taught it to boys from the palace school. Two of the most influential global styles — Iyengar Yoga and Ashtanga Vinyasa Yoga — descend from this teaching. In later life, in Madras, he emphasised adapting practice to the individual, a principle his son T.K.V. Desikachar developed as “Viniyoga” (Desikachar 1995).

Historians have shown that Krishnamacharya’s Mysore style drew not only on Haṭha texts but also on the physical culture of his time — Indian wrestlers’ exercises (vyāyāma), gymnastics and Western physical-culture systems then popular in India (Sjoman 1996; Singleton 2010). This is discussed further below.

docs.title: 11.4.5 B.K.S. Iyengar (1918–2014)
docs.text: B.K.S. Iyengar, Krishnamacharya’s brother-in-law and student, developed Iyengar Yoga, characterised by meticulous attention to alignment, the use of props (blocks, belts, blankets, bolsters, ropes) and a graded approach. His Light on Yoga (1966), which describes about 200 āsanas and 14 prāṇāyāmas with photographs, became a standard reference worldwide; it was followed by Light on Prāṇāyāma (1981) and The Tree of Yoga (1988) (Iyengar 1966, 1981, 1988). Among his students were the violinist Yehudi Menuhin, J. Krishnamurti and Queen Elisabeth of Belgium. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 2014, the year of his death.

docs.title: 11.4.6 K. Pattabhi Jois (1915–2009)
docs.text: K. Pattabhi Jois, another student of Krishnamacharya, codified Ashtanga Vinyasa Yoga, which he taught for six decades at his institute in Mysore. It consists of fixed series of āsanas performed in a set order, linked by breath (ujjāyī), bandha and gaze-points (dṛṣṭi). The Primary Series is called Yoga Cikitsā (“yoga therapy”) and the Intermediate Nāḍī Śodhana. Jois’s “Mysore style” self-practice attracted generations of Western students from the 1970s and gave rise to “Power Yoga” and many vinyasa-based styles. His legacy is now shadowed by accounts of sexual abuse, discussed in Section 11.10.

docs.title: 11.4.7 Swāmī Śivānanda (1887–1963) and His Disciples
docs.text: Swāmī Śivānanda Sarasvatī, born Kuppuswami, worked as a physician in Malaya before renouncing the world and settling in Rishikesh, where he founded the Divine Life Society in 1936. His eclectic “Yoga of Synthesis” combined Karma, Bhakti, Jñāna and Rāja Yoga, and he wrote some two hundred books. His disciples included Swāmī Satchidananda (Integral Yoga), Swāmī Vishnudevananda (Sivananda Yoga Vedanta Centres), Swāmī Chidananda, and Swāmī Satyānanda Sarasvatī, who founded the Bihar School of Yoga at Munger in the early 1960s; the school’s manuals on āsana, prāṇāyāma, mudrā and bandha are widely used (Satyananda Saraswati 1969; Sivananda 1935).

docs.title: 11.4.8 Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (1918–2008)
docs.text:
Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, a disciple of Swāmī Brahmānanda Sarasvatī, Śaṅkarācārya of Jyotirmaṭh, taught Transcendental Meditation (TM), a mantra-based technique presented as effortless and requiring no particular belief. TM attracted extensive scientific study from the 1970s; Herbert Benson’s research on meditation led to his concept of the “relaxation response” (Benson 1975). Much of the TM literature, however, was produced by researchers affiliated with the movement, and independent reviews have found its specific benefits over other relaxation methods to be uncertain (Table 11.1).

Table 11.1. Key Modern Yoga Teachers and Their Principal Contributions Teacher Dates Principal Contribution Swāmī Vivekānanda 1863–1902 Chicago 1893; Rāja Yoga; Ramakrishna Mission Paramahansa Yogananda 1893–1952 Kriyā Yoga; Autobiography of a Yogi; Self-Realization Fellowship Swāmī Kuvalayānanda 1883–1966 Kaivalyadhama (1924); early laboratory research on yoga T. Krishnamacharya 1888–1989 Mysore yogaśālā; vinyāsa; individualised teaching Swāmī Śivānanda 1887–1963 Divine Life Society; Yoga of Synthesis B.K.S. Iyengar 1918–2014 Iyengar Yoga; props; Light on Yoga K. Pattabhi Jois 1915–2009 Ashtanga Vinyasa Yoga; Mysore style Maharishi Mahesh Yogi 1918–2008 Transcendental Meditation

docs.title: 11.5 Women in the History of Yoga
docs.text:
Every teacher in Table 11.1 is a man, and almost every pre-modern yoga text was composed by men for male renunciants. Yet women have been present throughout the history of yoga, and in the modern period they have shaped it decisively.

Pre-modern sources. The Yogayājñavalkya, an influential Brahmanical yoga text (c. 13th–14th century), is framed as Yājñavalkya’s teaching of an eight-limbed yoga to the woman philosopher Gārgī, and it presents yoga as a discipline for householders as well as ascetics. Haṭha texts assume that women can practise: the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā describes a female form of vajrolī and calls the woman who masters it a yoginī (3.99, 3.102), and other texts teach their techniques to “women and men” alike (Mallinson and Singleton 2017). In Tantric traditions female deities and human yoginīs were central to ritual, and some Kaula lineages recognised women as initiates and teachers (White 2003). In Bengali Nātha legend Queen Mayanāmatī, a disciple of Gorakṣa, initiates her son Gopīcandra into the yogic life. The 14th-century Kashmiri Śaiva yoginī Lallā (Lal Ded) left Kashmiri verses (vākh) describing breath control, the central channel and the inner sound from her own practice (Hoskote 2011); and the women saints of Bhakti — Āṇṭāḷ, Akka Mahādevi, Mīrābāī — spoke of devotion as a yoga (Chapter 3).

The modern period. Indra Devi (Eugenie Peterson, 1899–2002), a Latvian-born actress, persuaded Krishnamacharya to teach her in Mysore in the late 1930s, becoming the first Western woman he trained; she taught in Shanghai, opened a studio in Hollywood in 1947, and later spread yoga across Latin America (Goldberg 2015). Through her and many others, posture yoga in the West became a practice taught and attended largely by women, and was adapted to women’s lives in ways the classical texts never considered. In India, Geeta S. Iyengar (1944–2018) developed sequences for menstruation, pregnancy and menopause in Yoga: A Gem for Women (1983), and women lead many of the institutions described in this chapter. The abuse cases discussed in Section 11.10 show the other side of this history: the students harmed by charismatic male teachers were very often women.
